title: Cell type versus reversible cell state
open: Determine which molecular differences define persistent neuronal or glial types and which reflect reversible activity, metabolic, developmental, or disease states. A solution should predict longitudinal identity and state transitions under controlled perturbations.
status: Whole-mouse-brain and adult-human-brain transcriptomic atlases greatly expanded classification in 2023, but static molecular clusters do not themselves resolve this distinction.
why: Establishes what a cell census should count and which classifications support causal experiments.
key_works: Yao et al. (2023), *A high-resolution transcriptomic and spatial atlas of cell types in the whole mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06812-z`; Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.

title: Cross-species cell-type homology
open: Establish a correspondence between cell types across species that distinguishes evolutionary homology from convergent molecular similarity. Validate correspondences using developmental lineage, connectivity, physiology, and perturbation responses.
status: Comparative cellular censuses provide candidate alignments; matching transcriptomic clusters is a partial result, not a complete evolutionary correspondence.
why: Determines which animal findings can legitimately be transferred to humans.
key_works: Krienen et al. (2023), *A marmoset brain cell census reveals regional specialization of cellular identities*, DOI: `10.1126/sciadv.adk3986`; Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.

title: Predicting physiology from molecular identity
open: Predict a cell’s intrinsic dynamics, synaptic integration, and neuromodulator responses from molecular measurements, including uncertainty and out-of-distribution failures.
status: Transcriptomic atlases and detailed human-neuron physiology supply complementary measurements, but neither establishes a general molecular-to-electrophysiological predictive law.
why: Would turn descriptive cell labels into executable biological models.
key_works: Yao et al. (2023), *A high-resolution transcriptomic and spatial atlas of cell types in the whole mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06812-z`; Gidon et al. (2020), *Dendritic action potentials and computation in human layer 2/3 cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aax6239`.

title: Functional proteome beyond the transcriptome
open: Construct matched measurements of RNA, protein abundance, protein localization, modification state, and physiology in identified cells. Determine which additional molecular layers materially improve functional prediction.
status: The 2023 brain atlases establish transcriptomic and regulatory reference points; a transcript count is not a measurement of localized functional protein.
why: Resolves discrepancies between molecular classification and actual cellular behavior.
key_works: Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`; Li et al. (2023), *A comparative atlas of single-cell chromatin accessibility in the human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.adf7044`.

title: Rare-cell and rare-region completeness
open: Estimate which human neural cell populations remain systematically undersampled, then obtain enough spatially resolved examples to distinguish rare types from artifacts and unusual states.
status: Large human and mouse atlases substantially reduce the gap, but their sampling designs do not certify discovery of every rare population across individuals and life stages.
why: Rare populations can be disproportionately important for disease or specialized functions.
key_works: Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`; Yao et al. (2023), *A high-resolution transcriptomic and spatial atlas of cell types in the whole mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06812-z`.

title: Noncoding variant-to-circuit causality
open: For a disease-associated noncoding variant, identify its causal regulatory element, target gene, relevant cell state, physiological consequence, and circuit-level effect. Validate the chain with allele-specific perturbation and rescue.
status: Human chromatin-accessibility atlases nominate regulatory mechanisms, but association and accessibility alone do not establish this causal chain.
why: Converts genetic association into actionable mechanisms.
key_works: Li et al. (2023), *A comparative atlas of single-cell chromatin accessibility in the human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.adf7044`.

title: Polygenic effects as physiological mechanisms
open: Determine how many small-effect variants combine to alter specific computations, rather than only predicting a diagnostic label. Test additive, epistatic, and cell-state-dependent models prospectively.
status: Large schizophrenia association studies identify many loci, but locus discovery does not yet supply a mechanistic composition rule.
why: Could make polygenic risk useful for biological stratification and intervention selection.
key_works: Trubetskoy et al. (2022), *Mapping genomic loci implicates genes and synaptic biology in schizophrenia*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04434-5`.

title: Somatic mutations that change neural function
open: Identify which acquired mutations in individual neurons or glia causally change physiology, cognition, or degeneration, and determine the clone sizes needed for measurable effects.
status: Single-neuron sequencing demonstrated informative somatic variation in 2015; detecting mutations is distinct from establishing their functional importance.
why: Tests whether mosaicism is mostly a lineage record, a disease mechanism, or both.
key_works: Lodato et al. (2015), *Somatic mutation in single human neurons tracks developmental and transcriptional history*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aab1785`.

title: Developmental lineage-to-connectivity mapping
open: Reconstruct neuronal lineage and synaptic connectivity in the same tissue, then determine which wiring properties are predicted by common ancestry independently of location and cell type.
status: Somatic lineage information and dense connectomics exist separately; their combination remains a demanding multimodal target.
why: Reveals how developmental history constrains circuit architecture.
key_works: Lodato et al. (2015), *Somatic mutation in single human neurons tracks developmental and transcriptional history*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aab1785`; MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`.

title: Durable information in neuronal chromatin
open: Determine whether particular activity-induced chromatin changes store behaviorally relevant information, merely permit plasticity, or reflect downstream consequences. Selective erasure and restoration must distinguish these possibilities.
status: Cell-specific chromatin maps reveal regulatory structure, but static accessibility does not establish an enduring memory-storage mechanism.
why: Could identify a durable substrate for long-term adaptation or pathological persistence.
key_works: Li et al. (2023), *A comparative atlas of single-cell chromatin accessibility in the human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.adf7044`; Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`.

title: Rules for synaptic nanocolumn alignment
open: Identify how presynaptic release machinery and postsynaptic receptors acquire, maintain, and modify nanoscale alignment. Predict the effect of moving specific components without changing their abundance.
status: Trans-synaptic nanocolumns were demonstrated in 2016; the general assembly and plasticity rules remain incompletely specified.
why: Links molecular geometry to synaptic efficacy.
key_works: Tang et al. (2016), *A trans-synaptic nanocolumn aligns neurotransmitter release to receptors*, DOI: `10.1038/nature19058`.

title: Release probability from molecular configuration
open: Predict release probability, multivesicular release, and short-term plasticity from measured active-zone architecture and molecular state at individual synapses.
status: Nanoscale alignment and vesicle-organization studies provide structural constraints, but not a generally validated probabilistic input-output model.
why: Supplies a missing parameterization for mechanistic circuit simulation.
key_works: Tang et al. (2016), *A trans-synaptic nanocolumn aligns neurotransmitter release to receptors*, DOI: `10.1038/nature19058`; Milovanovic et al. (2018), *A liquid phase of synapsin and lipid vesicles*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5671`.

title: Physiological functions of synaptic condensates
open: Determine when phase-separated synaptic assemblies are necessary for vesicle organization or plasticity in living brains. Perturb phase behavior separately from protein concentration and binding affinity.
status: Synapsin–vesicle phase separation was demonstrated in 2018; that result does not by itself establish the full in-vivo causal role.
why: Distinguishes a mechanistic organizational principle from an in-vitro analogy.
key_works: Milovanovic et al. (2018), *A liquid phase of synapsin and lipid vesicles*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5671`.

title: Molecular identity of synaptic tags
open: Identify the molecular states that mark specific synapses for later capture of plasticity-related products, including their lifetimes, specificity, and reset mechanisms.
status: Synaptic tagging was experimentally established in 1997; identifying a complete, context-general molecular implementation remains open.
why: Explains how a neuron directs broadly produced resources to selected synapses.
key_works: Frey and Morris (1997), *Synaptic tagging and long-term potentiation*, DOI: `10.1038/385533a0`.

title: Synaptic memory despite molecular turnover
open: Determine how a particular synaptic modification survives replacement of its constituent molecules. Demonstrate a maintenance mechanism that predicts both persistence and selective erasure.
status: Multiscale synaptic models provide favorable retention properties, but their biological state variables and renewal mechanisms remain to be established.
why: Addresses the mismatch between molecular lifetimes and memory lifetimes.
key_works: Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`; Frey and Morris (1997), *Synaptic tagging and long-term potentiation*, DOI: `10.1038/385533a0`.

title: Dendritic computations actually used during behavior
open: Determine which nonlinear dendritic operations are necessary for particular natural behaviors, rather than merely possible under controlled stimulation.
status: Human cortical dendrites exhibit powerful nonlinear computations ex vivo; their deployment during ordinary human behavior is not established by those experiments.
why: Tests whether neurons should be modeled as single units or structured computational networks.
key_works: Gidon et al. (2020), *Dendritic action potentials and computation in human layer 2/3 cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aax6239`; Poirazi, Brannon, and Mel (2003), *Pyramidal neuron as two-layer neural network*, DOI: `10.1016/S0896-6273(03)00149-1`.

title: Branch-specific inhibitory routing
open: Determine whether and how inhibition routes distinct information streams through individual dendritic branches. A solution should predict behavior-specific consequences of spatially targeted inhibitory perturbations.
status: Nonlinear dendritic physiology supplies a plausible substrate, but a general branch-level routing rule is not supplied by existing single-cell demonstrations.
why: Could explain flexible computation without changing anatomical connectivity.
key_works: Gidon et al. (2020), *Dendritic action potentials and computation in human layer 2/3 cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aax6239`; Poirazi, Brannon, and Mel (2003), *Pyramidal neuron as two-layer neural network*, DOI: `10.1016/S0896-6273(03)00149-1`.

title: Predicting spikes from complete synaptic input
open: Measure sufficiently complete excitatory, inhibitory, and modulatory input to predict a neuron’s spikes across behavioral states, with calibrated uncertainty.
status: High-fidelity human dendritic sodium spikes have been characterized, but recording every relevant input to an intact behaving neuron remains a separate measurement challenge.
why: Provides a stringent test of cellular models rather than fitting their outputs retrospectively.
key_works: Gooch et al. (2022), *High-fidelity dendritic sodium spike generation in human layer 2/3 neocortical pyramidal neurons*, DOI: `10.1016/j.celrep.2022.111500`.

title: Human-specific dendritic computational advantages
open: Identify which human–nonhuman dendritic differences change computational capability after controlling for morphology, age, tissue condition, and recording protocol.
status: Human dendritic nonlinearities and sodium-spike properties have been reported; a species-general comparative account of their functional advantages remains incomplete.
why: Tests proposed cellular contributions to human cognition.
key_works: Gidon et al. (2020), *Dendritic action potentials and computation in human layer 2/3 cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aax6239`; Gooch et al. (2022), *High-fidelity dendritic sodium spike generation in human layer 2/3 neocortical pyramidal neurons*, DOI: `10.1016/j.celrep.2022.111500`.

title: Dendrites as biological credit-assignment machinery
open: Establish whether compartment-specific signals carry instructive errors or targets for learning, and derive learning rules that match measured dendritic and synaptic changes.
status: Biologically motivated learning algorithms demonstrate computational possibilities; they do not establish that a specific dendritic implementation operates in vivo.
why: Connects cellular physiology to efficient learning.
key_works: Bellec et al. (2020), *A solution to the learning dilemma for recurrent networks of spiking neurons*, DOI: `10.1038/s41467-020-17236-y`; Song et al. (2024), *Inferring neural activity before plasticity as a foundation for learning beyond backpropagation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01514-1`.

title: Activity-dependent myelin timing rules
subfield: Axons, myelin, and nonsynaptic electrical interactions
open: Determine how neural activity controls internode placement, length, and thickness to tune conduction delays. Predict which temporal relationships are optimized during learning.
status: Motor learning requires new myelination in mouse experiments, and timing-related consequences have been demonstrated; the adaptation rule remains unresolved.
why: Adds adaptive transmission delays to models of learning.
key_works: McKenzie et al. (2014), *Motor skill learning requires active central myelination*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1254960`; Kato et al. (2020), *Motor learning requires myelination to reduce asynchrony and spontaneity in neural activity*, DOI: `10.1002/glia.23713`.

title: Myelin’s timing versus metabolic contributions
subfield: Axons, myelin, and nonsynaptic electrical interactions
open: Separate myelin-dependent changes in conduction from changes in axonal metabolic support, and quantify their respective contributions to learning and long-term survival.
status: Learning-related myelination is causally implicated, but disrupting myelin-related processes can affect several functions simultaneously.
why: Determines which myelin functions therapies must restore.
key_works: McKenzie et al. (2014), *Motor skill learning requires active central myelination*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1254960`; Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`.

title: Branch-specific axonal transmission reliability
subfield: Axons, myelin, and nonsynaptic electrical interactions
open: Measure when an action potential successfully invades every branch of an identified axon during natural activity, and predict branch-specific failures or timing changes.
status: Dense connectomes establish branching geometry, but anatomical continuity does not establish reliable, state-independent transmission to every terminal.
why: Tests whether an axon broadcasts one identical message to all targets.
key_works: MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`; Kato et al. (2020), *Motor learning requires myelination to reduce asynchrony and spontaneity in neural activity*, DOI: `10.1002/glia.23713`.

title: Functionally precise remyelination
subfield: Axons, myelin, and nonsynaptic electrical interactions
open: Restore damaged myelin with conduction delays and metabolic support appropriate to the original circuit, rather than demonstrating myelin formation alone.
status: Evidence linking myelination to coordinated activity makes timing fidelity a distinct repair target beyond histological remyelination.
why: May determine whether structural repair actually restores coordinated behavior.
key_works: Kato et al. (2020), *Motor learning requires myelination to reduce asynchrony and spontaneity in neural activity*, DOI: `10.1002/glia.23713`; McKenzie et al. (2014), *Motor skill learning requires active central myelination*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1254960`.

title: Behavioral necessity of ephaptic coupling
subfield: Axons, myelin, and nonsynaptic electrical interactions
open: Determine when endogenous extracellular fields contribute causally to computation independently of chemical synapses and gap junctions. Establish effect sizes under physiological conditions with selective perturbations.
status: Cortical ephaptic effects were demonstrated in 2011; their existence is not the open question, but their circuit-specific computational necessity remains unresolved.
why: Tests whether conventional synaptic network descriptions omit consequential interactions.
key_works: Anastassiou et al. (2011), *Ephaptic coupling of cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.2727`.

title: Predictive developmental wiring code
open: Predict which individual neurons will connect from lineage, molecular recognition, geometry, and developmental activity. Validate predictions after altering one component of the developmental program.
status: Modern cell atlases and connectomes provide endpoints, but they do not constitute a generative developmental wiring law.
why: Connects developmental biology to mature circuit architecture.
key_works: Yao et al. (2023), *A high-resolution transcriptomic and spatial atlas of cell types in the whole mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06812-z`; Dorkenwald et al. (2024), *Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-024-07558-y`.

title: Individual cortical folding from growth mechanisms
open: Predict an individual brain’s folding trajectory from measured tissue growth, mechanics, and regional developmental programs, including malformations and uncertainty.
status: Physical growth models reproduced important folding features in 2016; they are not a complete patient-specific developmental predictor.
why: Links cellular growth abnormalities to brain-scale anatomy.
key_works: Tallinen et al. (2016), *On the growth and form of cortical convolutions*, DOI: `10.1038/nphys3632`.

title: Selective reopening of critical periods
open: Reopen a specified plasticity window in adults without destabilizing established skills or producing unwanted learning. Demonstrate targeted, durable functional improvement.
status: Psychedelics reopened a social-reward learning critical period in mice in 2023; generalization to other systems and safe human selectivity remains open.
why: Could enable rehabilitation while avoiding indiscriminate plasticity.
key_works: Nardou et al. (2023), *Psychedelics reopen the social reward learning critical period*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06204-3`.

title: Instructive content of spontaneous developmental activity
open: Determine which features of spontaneous activity instruct wiring and which simply permit maturation. Replace native patterns with controlled alternatives and test predicted wiring changes.
status: Activity-dependent synapse elimination provides a causal foothold, but does not specify the information carried by developmental activity patterns.
why: Distinguishes self-generated training signals from generic trophic activity.
key_works: Schafer et al. (2012), *Microglia sculpt postnatal neural circuits in an activity and complement-dependent manner*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.026`.

title: Timing-specific developmental vulnerability
open: Determine why the same genetic or environmental perturbation has different consequences at different developmental stages. Predict vulnerable windows for defined cell populations and functions.
status: Autism genetics implicates both developmental and functional processes; identifying genes does not resolve when their perturbation becomes consequential.
why: Makes prevention and intervention timing mechanistically grounded.
key_works: Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`.

title: Context-specific necessity of gliotransmission
open: Determine which astrocyte populations release transmitters under physiological conditions and when that release is necessary for circuit computation or behavior.
status: A specialized glutamatergic astrocyte population was reported in 2023; this does not establish universal glutamate release by astrocytes.
why: Resolves a major mechanistic dispute without treating astrocytes as a uniform class.
key_works: de Ceglia et al. (2023), *Specialized astrocytes mediate glutamatergic gliotransmission in the CNS*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06502-w`.

title: Astrocytic microdomain integration
open: Determine how local signals in fine astrocytic processes combine, remain independent, or trigger larger responses. Predict their spatial and temporal influence on nearby synapses.
status: Identification of functionally specialized astrocytes sharpens the question, but population identity does not specify computation within an individual astrocyte.
why: Establishes the appropriate computational units for astrocyte models.
key_works: de Ceglia et al. (2023), *Specialized astrocytes mediate glutamatergic gliotransmission in the CNS*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06502-w`.

title: Lactate as fuel versus signal
open: Separate the energetic and signaling roles of astrocyte-derived lactate during memory formation. Quantify relevant fluxes and perform rescues that discriminate the mechanisms.
status: Astrocyte–neuron lactate transport was causally implicated in long-term memory in 2011; that result does not settle all transport directions or signaling functions.
why: Determines what metabolic interventions must actually replace.
key_works: Suzuki et al. (2011), *Astrocyte-neuron lactate transport is required for long-term memory formation*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2011.02.018`.

title: Astrocyte state-to-function mapping
open: Map molecular astrocyte states to measurable effects on synapses, metabolism, vascular regulation, and repair, including transitions within the same cells.
status: Cell atlases and specialized-gliotransmission findings provide candidate subdivisions, but not a comprehensive functional state-transition map.
why: Replaces broad “reactive astrocyte” labels with testable functions.
key_works: Yao et al. (2023), *A high-resolution transcriptomic and spatial atlas of cell types in the whole mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06812-z`; de Ceglia et al. (2023), *Specialized astrocytes mediate glutamatergic gliotransmission in the CNS*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06502-w`.

title: Astrocyte-mediated resource allocation
open: Determine whether astrocytes allocate metabolic support according to local activity, predicted demand, or competitive rules. Test whether these rules influence which synapses can learn.
status: Lactate-transport experiments connect astrocytic metabolism to memory, but do not establish a resource-allocation algorithm across competing synapses.
why: Connects metabolic constraints to learning selectivity.
key_works: Suzuki et al. (2011), *Astrocyte-neuron lactate transport is required for long-term memory formation*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2011.02.018`; Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`.

title: Synapse-specific selection for elimination
open: Identify the combination of activity, complement, surface signals, and microglial state that determines whether a particular synapse is removed or spared.
status: Complement-dependent elimination and activity-dependent microglial pruning were established in 2007–2012; a predictive synapse-by-synapse selection rule remains open.
why: Enables targeted preservation or removal of connections.
key_works: Stevens et al. (2007), *The classical complement cascade mediates CNS synapse elimination*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2007.10.036`; Schafer et al. (2012), *Microglia sculpt postnatal neural circuits in an activity and complement-dependent manner*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.026`.

title: Protective versus destructive microglial programs
open: Identify interventions that suppress harmful microglial actions while preserving pathogen control, debris removal, and repair. Validate the separation across disease stages.
status: Microglia can be protective during infection, while complement-associated synapse elimination provides a different functional pathway; “turning microglia off” is not a mechanism-specific solution.
why: Avoids therapies that remove beneficial immune functions.
key_works: Wheeler et al. (2018), *Microglia are required for protection against lethal coronavirus encephalitis in mice*, DOI: `10.1172/JCI97229`; Stevens et al. (2007), *The classical complement cascade mediates CNS synapse elimination*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2007.10.036`.

title: Long-lived immune memory in the brain
open: Determine which persistent microglial or border-immune changes encode prior infection, stress, or injury, and whether resetting them changes later neurological vulnerability.
status: Infection studies establish important microglial responses, but acute protection does not explain the persistence or causal consequences of later immune states.
why: Could explain delayed effects of earlier inflammatory events.
key_works: Wheeler et al. (2018), *Microglia are required for protection against lethal coronavirus encephalitis in mice*, DOI: `10.1172/JCI97229`; Li et al. (2023), *A comparative atlas of single-cell chromatin accessibility in the human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.adf7044`.

title: Meningeal immune-to-circuit signaling
open: Map the routes and conditions through which meningeal immune and lymphatic processes alter specific neural circuits. Separate drainage effects from cytokine, vascular, and neural signaling.
status: Meningeal lymphatic vessels were characterized in 2015; their existence does not establish a complete causal map to cognition or behavior.
why: Connects peripheral immunity and brain function through defined mechanisms.
key_works: Louveau et al. (2015), *Structural and functional features of central nervous system lymphatic vessels*, DOI: `10.1038/nature14432`.

title: Epstein–Barr virus-to-multiple-sclerosis mechanism
open: Determine which events after Epstein–Barr virus infection lead to multiple sclerosis in susceptible people, and which intervention interrupts that causal pathway.
status: A major longitudinal study strengthened the association in 2022; the remaining problem is not whether an association exists, but the intervening mechanism and preventive leverage.
why: Could support mechanism-based prevention rather than treatment after substantial injury.
key_works: Bjornevik et al. (2022), *Longitudinal analysis reveals high prevalence of Epstein-Barr virus associated with multiple sclerosis*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abj8222`.

title: Reconciling sleep-dependent clearance measurements
open: Reconcile apparently conflicting sleep-clearance results using matched tracers, compartments, behavioral states, and transport models. Distinguish tracer entry, redistribution, and actual elimination.
status: A 2024 study reported reduced clearance during sleep and anesthesia; a 2025 study implicated sleep-related vasomotion in glymphatic clearance. The assays and mechanisms require direct reconciliation.
why: Determines whether proposed clearance therapies target the correct process.
key_works: Miao et al. (2024), *Brain clearance is reduced during sleep and anesthesia*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-024-01638-y`; Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`.

title: Convection versus diffusion in brain solute transport
open: Quantify the relative contributions of diffusion, bulk flow, dispersion, and compartment exchange to transport of molecules of different sizes in living brain tissue.
status: Sleep-clearance and vasomotion experiments constrain transport, but a single tracer measurement cannot identify all underlying transport mechanisms.
why: Establishes which physical interventions could materially change clearance.
key_works: Xie et al. (2013), *Sleep drives metabolite clearance from the adult brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1241224`; Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`.

title: Noninvasive human clearance quantification
open: Develop a validated, repeatable human measurement of brain solute elimination that does not depend on invasive tracer administration and distinguishes relevant compartments.
status: Mechanistic animal studies and anatomical drainage discoveries provide foundations, but their measurements are not automatically transferable to routine human monitoring.
why: Makes clearance hypotheses testable in longitudinal human studies.
key_works: Louveau et al. (2015), *Structural and functional features of central nervous system lymphatic vessels*, DOI: `10.1038/nature14432`; Miao et al. (2024), *Brain clearance is reduced during sleep and anesthesia*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-024-01638-y`.

title: State-dependent neurovascular transfer functions
open: Predict the vascular response to identified neural and glial activity across sleep, attention, aging, and disease, rather than assuming one fixed neural-to-hemodynamic relationship.
status: Sleep-related vascular dynamics demonstrate relevant state dependence; mapping this to quantitative interpretation of human imaging remains a separate problem.
why: Improves interpretation of functional imaging and vascular contributions to disease.
key_works: Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`; Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`.

title: Cell-selective barrier repair
open: Restore a damaged brain barrier’s transport and immune selectivity without indiscriminately preventing beneficial exchange or producing pathological closure.
status: Molecular atlases improve the cellular starting point, but identifying barrier-associated cells is not equivalent to controlling barrier function in a disease-specific manner.
why: Enables safer treatment of leakage, inflammation, and drug-delivery failures.
key_works: Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`; Louveau et al. (2015), *Structural and functional features of central nervous system lymphatic vessels*, DOI: `10.1038/nature14432`.

title: Synapse-resolved energy budgets in vivo
open: Measure ATP production and consumption at identified synapses during behavior, including the costs of signaling, plasticity, maintenance, and failed transmission.
status: Quantitative energy budgets and experiments linking local ATP synthesis to synaptic function provide foundations; a behaviorally resolved accounting remains incomplete.
why: Reveals which computations are limited by local energy availability.
key_works: Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`; Rangaraju, Calloway, and Ryan (2014), *Activity-driven local ATP synthesis is required for synaptic function*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2013.12.042`.

title: Mitochondrial placement as a computational constraint
open: Determine whether mitochondrial trafficking and local reserve capacity predict which branches or synapses can sustain high activity and learning. Test causal relocation independently of overall mitochondrial health.
status: Local ATP synthesis is functionally important, but this does not specify an optimal placement or trafficking rule for extended neurons.
why: Connects organelle logistics to information processing.
key_works: Rangaraju, Calloway, and Ryan (2014), *Activity-driven local ATP synthesis is required for synaptic function*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2013.12.042`.

title: Causal functions of regional brain lipid composition
open: Determine which regional lipid patterns causally affect excitability, synaptic organization, and vulnerability, rather than merely marking cell composition.
status: A spatial mouse-brain lipid atlas was published in September 2026; mapping lipid distributions is a milestone, not a complete functional explanation.
why: Opens intervention targets not captured by transcriptomics alone.
key_works: Fusar Bassini et al. (2026), *The lipidomic architecture of the mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-026-11050-0`.

title: Dynamic intercellular lipid-flux atlas
open: Measure synthesis, transfer, remodeling, and degradation of defined lipids between neurons and glia during learning, aging, and injury.
status: The 2026 lipid atlas establishes spatial organization, but a static abundance map is not a measurement of intercellular flux.
why: Distinguishes lipid supply failures from altered use or clearance.
key_works: Fusar Bassini et al. (2026), *The lipidomic architecture of the mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-026-11050-0`.

title: Energy–accuracy–latency bounds for neural computation
open: Derive biologically constrained bounds connecting energy use, inference accuracy, response time, and reliability. Determine how close identifiable circuits operate to those bounds.
status: Classical neural energy budgets quantify important costs; they do not establish general optimality limits for natural computations.
why: Separates avoidable inefficiency from physical limits.
key_works: Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`; Moreno-Bote et al. (2014), *Information-limiting correlations*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3807`.

title: Complete mammalian synapse-resolved connectome
open: Reconstruct a complete mammalian nervous-system circuit at synaptic resolution, with explicit error estimates, biological metadata, and reproducible access.
status: An adult fly brain was mapped in 2024; MICrONS delivered approximately cubic-millimeter-scale mouse cortical functional connectomics in 2025. Neither is a complete mammalian connectome.
why: Enables genuinely brain-wide tests of anatomical network hypotheses.
key_works: Dorkenwald et al. (2024), *Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-024-07558-y`; MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`.

title: Predicting activity from a connectome
open: Predict neural responses and behavioral effects of unseen interventions from measured wiring plus explicitly specified additional biological variables.
status: MICrONS aligns structure and activity, while the worm signal-propagation atlas supplies perturbational measurements; anatomical mapping alone does not solve functional prediction.
why: Tests what explanatory information a connectome actually contains.
key_works: MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`; Randi et al. (2023), *Neural signal propagation atlas of Caenorhabditis elegans*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06683-4`.

title: Extrasynaptic and modulatory connectomes
open: Map functional communication mediated by neuromodulators, volume transmission, and other nonsynaptic routes, including receptor state and spatial reach.
status: The worm propagation atlas demonstrates the value of measuring effective communication rather than inferring all influence from synaptic edges.
why: Prevents anatomically complete maps from being functionally incomplete.
key_works: Randi et al. (2023), *Neural signal propagation atlas of Caenorhabditis elegans*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06683-4`; Anastassiou et al. (2011), *Ephaptic coupling of cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.2727`.

title: Longitudinal synapse-resolved connectomics
open: Track synapse formation, disappearance, and remodeling in the same substantial circuit while preserving functional measurements and cell identities.
status: Dense electron-microscopy connectomes provide exceptional structural detail but are endpoint measurements; chronic activity studies do not recover the same complete synaptic graph.
why: Makes structural learning and degeneration directly observable.
key_works: Dorkenwald et al. (2024), *Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-024-07558-y`; Ziv et al. (2013), *Long-term dynamics of CA1 hippocampal place codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3329`.

title: Tenfold cheaper verified connectomics
open: Reduce total acquisition, reconstruction, proofreading, storage, and access cost by at least tenfold against a preregistered baseline while maintaining measured synapse and connectivity error rates.
status: Proposed moonshot; MICrONS supplies a substantial real pipeline against which component and end-to-end improvements can be measured.
why: Makes replication across animals, conditions, and laboratories feasible.
key_works: MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`.

title: Information-limiting correlations in natural behavior
open: Determine which correlations actually limit behaviorally available information in large populations, rather than merely appearing in finite recordings.
status: Theoretical information-limiting correlations were characterized in 2014; identifying and estimating their real biological contribution remains difficult.
why: Determines whether adding neurons improves information or mainly adds redundancy.
key_works: Moreno-Bote et al. (2014), *Information-limiting correlations*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3807`.

title: Neural code timescale selection
open: Determine when downstream circuits use precise spike timing, spike counts, population trajectories, or mixtures of these, and predict task-dependent switches.
status: Population dynamics and information-theoretic results establish useful descriptions, but do not identify one universally relevant temporal code.
why: Defines what recording resolution and decoder assumptions are biologically justified.
key_works: Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`; Moreno-Bote et al. (2014), *Information-limiting correlations*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3807`.

title: Representation of uncertainty
open: Distinguish probabilistic population codes, sampling-based representations, and deterministic alternatives using predictions about single-trial dynamics and causal perturbations.
status: Brain-wide studies identify prior-information representations, but observing prior-related activity does not settle the neural format of uncertainty.
why: Explains confidence, inference, exploration, and decision variability.
key_works: Ma et al. (2006), *Bayesian inference with probabilistic population codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn1790`; Findling et al. (2025), *Brain-wide representations of prior information in mouse decision-making*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09226-1`.

title: True dimensionality of neural representations
open: Estimate representational dimensionality and spectral structure while correcting for noise, finite trials, stimulus sampling, and behavioral confounds.
status: A 2019 visual-cortex study reported high-dimensional geometry; a 2025 reanalysis sharpened concerns about estimating those properties reliably.
why: Tests claims about coding efficiency, generalization, and neural manifold structure.
key_works: Stringer et al. (2019), *High-dimensional geometry of population responses in visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1346-5`; Pospisil and Pillow (2025), *Revisiting the high-dimensional geometry of population responses in the visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2506535122`.

title: Binding distributed features into individual objects
open: Identify the mechanism that assigns distributed features to the correct object or event, especially when several similar objects are simultaneously present.
status: Large-scale population descriptions reveal distributed representations, but representational geometry alone does not specify feature-to-object assignment.
why: Explains compositional perception without confusing features from different sources.
key_works: Stringer et al. (2019), *High-dimensional geometry of population responses in visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1346-5`; Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`.

title: General biological credit assignment
open: Derive and experimentally validate a local learning mechanism that assigns credit across recurrent circuits, delayed outcomes, and multiple interacting brain regions.
status: E-prop provides a computationally effective eligibility-trace approach; it is not a general experimental identification of the brain’s learning rule.
why: Connects synaptic change to successful learning of complex behavior.
key_works: Bellec et al. (2020), *A solution to the learning dilemma for recurrent networks of spiking neurons*, DOI: `10.1038/s41467-020-17236-y`.

title: Learning without symmetric feedback weights
open: Establish when biologically realistic asymmetric feedback can support accurate multilayer learning, and identify conditions where it provably cannot.
status: Feedback alignment and inference-based learning supply partial computational solutions; their biological implementation and general guarantees remain open.
why: Tests whether a central obstacle to biologically plausible learning is fundamental or architectural.
key_works: Lillicrap et al. (2016), *Random synaptic feedback weights support error backpropagation for deep learning*, DOI: `10.1038/ncomms13276`; Song et al. (2024), *Inferring neural activity before plasticity as a foundation for learning beyond backpropagation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01514-1`.

title: Capacity–lifetime tradeoffs in biological memory
open: Derive sharp storage-capacity and retention bounds for synapses with realistic noise, turnover, bounded molecular resources, and continual learning.
status: Multiscale consolidation models achieve strong theoretical retention properties; matching their assumptions and limits to biology remains unresolved.
why: Separates architectural limitations from remediable biological failures.
key_works: Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`.

title: Homeostasis without erasing learned structure
open: Determine how neurons stabilize activity while preserving useful relative synaptic changes. A solution must predict responses to prolonged perturbation and continued learning.
status: Circuit degeneracy and consolidation models show that stable outputs and persistent memories can arise in different ways; a unified biological rule remains open.
why: Explains how brains remain stable without becoming unable to learn.
key_works: Prinz, Bucher, and Marder (2004), *Similar network activity from disparate circuit parameters*, DOI: `10.1038/nn1352`; Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`.

title: Molecular implementation of behavioral-timescale plasticity
open: Identify the eligibility traces and instructive signals that associate inputs with events separated by seconds, and determine where the same rule applies outside hippocampal place learning.
status: Behavioral-timescale synaptic plasticity was demonstrated in CA1 in 2017; its complete molecular implementation and scope remain open.
why: Explains rapid learning from temporally extended experience.
key_works: Bittner et al. (2017), *Behavioral time scale synaptic plasticity underlies CA1 place fields*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aan3846`.

title: Genuine neural criticality versus statistical lookalikes
open: Distinguish true critical dynamics from noncritical systems that produce similar avalanche distributions through subsampling, filtering, or external drive.
status: Neuronal avalanches were reported in 2003; power-law-like observations alone do not settle the underlying dynamical regime.
why: Tests a major proposed organizing principle of neural activity.
key_works: Beggs and Plenz (2003), *Neuronal avalanches in neocortical circuits*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.23-35-11167.2003`.

title: Causal computational benefits of criticality
open: Move an identified circuit toward and away from a measured critical regime while controlling confounds, then test predicted changes in learning, sensitivity, and robustness.
status: Avalanche observations motivate the hypothesis; demonstrating a distributional signature is distinct from proving a behavioral advantage.
why: Determines whether criticality is functional, incidental, or task-dependent.
key_works: Beggs and Plenz (2003), *Neuronal avalanches in neocortical circuits*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.23-35-11167.2003`.

title: Circuit identifiability under degeneracy
open: Characterize which combinations of anatomical, electrophysiological, and perturbational measurements uniquely identify circuit parameters, and which leave unavoidable equivalence classes.
status: Distinct parameter sets producing similar activity were demonstrated in 2004; the open target is a general identifiability theory for realistic circuits.
why: Prevents overinterpreting a successful fitted model as the unique mechanism.
key_works: Prinz, Bucher, and Marder (2004), *Similar network activity from disparate circuit parameters*, DOI: `10.1038/nn1352`.

title: Stable behavior with drifting neural representations
open: Determine how downstream readers maintain stable behavior while upstream population codes change. Distinguish coordinated drift, redundant coding, and continuous decoder adaptation.
status: Longitudinal hippocampal recordings documented changing place codes in 2013; recording drift does not explain successful downstream readout.
why: Explains lifelong reliability despite biological change.
key_works: Ziv et al. (2013), *Long-term dynamics of CA1 hippocampal place codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3329`.

title: Effective communication across distributed brain activity
open: Determine when activity in one region actually changes another region’s computation rather than merely covarying with a shared behavioral variable.
status: The 2025 brain-wide mouse activity map greatly expands coverage across regions and laboratories, but broad representation is not equivalent to directed causal communication.
why: Separates information availability from information use.
key_works: International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`.

title: Recurrent computation in difficult object recognition
open: Identify which recurrent interactions are necessary for recognizing occluded, ambiguous, or unfamiliar objects, and predict failures from targeted circuit perturbations.
status: Performance-optimized models explain important visual responses, but predictive fit does not establish the causal recurrent algorithm.
why: Connects visual robustness to specific circuit mechanisms.
key_works: Yamins et al. (2014), *Performance-optimized hierarchical models predict neural responses in higher visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.1403112111`; MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`.

title: Predictive coding versus alternative mismatch mechanisms
open: Design interventions that distinguish explicit prediction-error computation from adaptation, movement feedback, and other mechanisms producing mismatch responses.
status: Sensorimotor mismatch signals were reported in mouse visual cortex in 2012; the response alone does not uniquely identify a predictive-coding architecture.
why: Tests a widely used explanatory framework with discriminating predictions.
key_works: Keller, Bonhoeffer, and Hübener (2012), *Sensorimotor mismatch signals in primary visual cortex of the behaving mouse*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.040`; Rao and Ballard (1999), *Predictive coding in the visual cortex: a functional interpretation of some extra-classical receptive-field effects*, DOI: `10.1038/4580`.

title: Visual models that generalize beyond benchmark images
open: Predict neural responses and behavior for novel scene statistics, active viewing, unusual viewpoints, and visual illusions without task-specific refitting.
status: Hierarchical models achieve substantial predictive success, while population-geometry work exposes the importance of stimulus and noise sampling.
why: Tests whether models explain vision rather than a particular dataset.
key_works: Yamins et al. (2014), *Performance-optimized hierarchical models predict neural responses in higher visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.1403112111`; Pospisil and Pillow (2025), *Revisiting the high-dimensional geometry of population responses in the visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2506535122`.

title: Wiring rules that create visual invariance
open: Determine which measured connectivity motifs generate tolerance to translation, scale, pose, and illumination, and which invariances require learning or feedback.
status: Functional connectomics now permits direct structure–response comparisons, but motif identification is not yet a complete generative account of invariance.
why: Links visual computations to physical circuit design.
key_works: MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`; Yamins et al. (2014), *Performance-optimized hierarchical models predict neural responses in higher visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.1403112111`.

title: Active vision’s sampling policy
open: Explain how eye, head, and body movements are selected to acquire task-relevant visual information, including how neural uncertainty influences the next movement.
status: Sensorimotor mismatch experiments establish interaction between movement and visual input, but do not identify a general information-acquisition policy.
why: Replaces passive-image descriptions with an account of natural seeing.
key_works: Keller, Bonhoeffer, and Hübener (2012), *Sensorimotor mismatch signals in primary visual cortex of the behaving mouse*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.040`.

title: Causal selection of one speaker in a crowd
open: Identify how attention selects one speaker’s representation while preserving the ability to switch targets, and determine the causal contributions of auditory and control circuits.
status: Selective cortical representation of an attended speaker was demonstrated in 2012; a representation does not itself establish the selection mechanism.
why: Explains a central limitation of real-world hearing.
key_works: Mesgarani and Chang (2012), *Selective cortical representation of attended speaker in multi-talker speech perception*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11020`.

title: Reliable human cochlear-synaptopathy diagnosis
open: Develop a noninvasive marker that quantifies cochlear synapse loss in an individual and predicts specific hearing difficulties independently of other auditory damage.
status: Mouse work established lasting neural degeneration after apparently temporary noise-related threshold changes in 2009; individual human quantification remains a distinct challenge.
why: Makes otherwise hidden injury measurable before major threshold loss.
key_works: Kujawa and Liberman (2009), *Adding insult to injury: cochlear nerve degeneration after “temporary” noise-induced hearing loss*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2845-09.2009`.

title: Functionally precise auditory synapse regeneration
open: Regenerate damaged hair-cell–auditory-nerve connections with appropriate tuning, timing, and central integration, then demonstrate improved natural listening.
status: Identification of persistent cochlear neural injury establishes the repair target; synapse formation alone would not demonstrate restored auditory coding.
why: Could restore hearing functions that amplification cannot replace.
key_works: Kujawa and Liberman (2009), *Adding insult to injury: cochlear nerve degeneration after “temporary” noise-induced hearing loss*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2845-09.2009`.

title: Individual tinnitus mechanisms
open: Determine which combinations of peripheral injury, central gain, prediction, and affective learning sustain tinnitus in a particular person, and prospectively select an effective intervention.
status: Peripheral deafferentation and cortical auditory-selection studies constrain possible mechanisms, but neither supplies a universal tinnitus explanation.
why: Replaces a heterogeneous symptom label with actionable mechanisms.
key_works: Kujawa and Liberman (2009), *Adding insult to injury: cochlear nerve degeneration after “temporary” noise-induced hearing loss*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2845-09.2009`; Mesgarani and Chang (2012), *Selective cortical representation of attended speaker in multi-talker speech perception*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11020`.

title: Auditory generalization across speakers and environments
open: Explain how neural circuits preserve linguistic and sound-source identity across accents, unfamiliar voices, reverberation, and background noise.
status: Attended-speech representations and language-model alignment provide partial descriptions; they do not establish a complete causal account of acoustic generalization.
why: Links robust hearing to learnable transformations rather than memorized acoustics.
key_works: Mesgarani and Chang (2012), *Selective cortical representation of attended speaker in multi-talker speech perception*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11020`; Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`.

title: Molecule-to-odor prediction through biological mechanisms
open: Predict odor percepts from molecular structure through receptor activation and neural processing, including unfamiliar molecules and explicit uncertainty.
status: The 2023 principal odor map improved diverse perceptual predictions; predictive embeddings do not yet establish the complete receptor-to-percept causal chain.
why: Connects chemistry to perception and enables rational sensory design.
key_works: Lee et al. (2023), *A principal odor map unifies diverse tasks in olfactory perception*, DOI: `10.1126/science.ade4401`.

title: Nonlinear perception of odor mixtures
open: Predict when mixtures are perceived elementally, configurally, or suppressively from component identity, concentration, and prior exposure.
status: Single-molecule perceptual models and receptor-interaction studies supply pieces of the problem; mixture perception is not reducible to averaging component descriptors.
why: Most natural olfactory environments contain mixtures.
key_works: Lee et al. (2023), *A principal odor map unifies diverse tasks in olfactory perception*, DOI: `10.1126/science.ade4401`; Fukutani et al. (2023), *Antagonistic interactions between odorants alter human odor perception* (verify bibliographic identifier).

title: Learning-dependent odor identity and valence
open: Determine which circuit changes alter an odor’s identity representation versus its learned pleasantness, threat value, or motivational significance.
status: Perceptual odor maps provide a baseline organization, but do not explain how experience transforms identity and value separately.
why: Distinguishes sensory remapping from associative learning.
key_works: Lee et al. (2023), *A principal odor map unifies diverse tasks in olfactory perception*, DOI: `10.1126/science.ade4401`; Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`.

title: Taste, postingestive feedback, and nutrient value
open: Determine how oral taste signals and delayed gut feedback jointly establish nutrient preferences, including dissociations between sensory sweetness and physiological value.
status: A rapid gut-to-brain nutrient-sensing circuit was demonstrated in 2018; integrating that pathway with taste and long-term preference learning remains open.
why: Explains food choice beyond immediate taste.
key_works: Kaelberer et al. (2018), *A gut-brain neural circuit for nutrient sensory transduction*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5236`.

title: Individual differences in chemical perception
open: Predict person-specific odor and taste percepts from receptor variation, experience, physiological state, and exposure history.
status: Population-level odor prediction is substantially improved, but a shared perceptual map does not fully explain individual deviations.
why: Enables personalized sensory diagnostics and reproducible cross-population studies.
key_works: Lee et al. (2023), *A principal odor map unifies diverse tasks in olfactory perception*, DOI: `10.1126/science.ade4401`.

title: Mechanotransduction-to-touch population code
subfield: Touch, proprioception, vestibular processing, and multisensory integration
open: Predict tactile percepts from skin mechanics, receptor activation, and population activity, including changes caused by force direction, speed, and contact geometry.
status: PIEZO2’s major role in touch was established in mice and its importance in human mechanosensation demonstrated clinically; the full population code remains open.
why: Connects mechanical contact to perception and prosthetic feedback.
key_works: Ranade et al. (2014), *Piezo2 is the major transducer of mechanical forces for touch sensation in mice*, DOI: `10.1038/nature13980`; Chesler et al. (2016), *The Role of PIEZO2 in Human Mechanosensation*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1602812`.

title: Construction of a whole-body state estimate
subfield: Touch, proprioception, vestibular processing, and multisensory integration
open: Explain how proprioceptive, vestibular, visual, and motor-command signals produce a coherent estimate of body configuration and uncertainty.
status: Human PIEZO2 deficiency provides a causal probe of proprioceptive contributions, but not a complete algorithm for body-state estimation.
why: Supports rehabilitation and embodied control.
key_works: Chesler et al. (2016), *The Role of PIEZO2 in Human Mechanosensation*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1602812`.

title: Individual vestibular compensation
subfield: Touch, proprioception, vestibular processing, and multisensory integration
open: Predict how and when the nervous system reweights sensory information after vestibular injury, and identify interventions that improve adaptation without inducing maladaptive dependence.
status: Studies of disrupted mechanosensation demonstrate substantial multisensory compensation, but do not provide a patient-specific vestibular recovery model.
why: Addresses persistent imbalance and motion intolerance.
key_works: Chesler et al. (2016), *The Role of PIEZO2 in Human Mechanosensation*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1602812`; Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`.

title: Multisensory temporal binding
subfield: Touch, proprioception, vestibular processing, and multisensory integration
open: Determine how circuits decide whether signals with different delays arise from the same event, and how those temporal windows adapt to experience and context.
status: Neural models can represent distributed sensory information, but identifying the causal mechanism for common-event assignment remains distinct from decoding each modality.
why: Explains coherent perception despite unequal sensory latencies.
key_works: Mesgarani and Chang (2012), *Selective cortical representation of attended speaker in multi-talker speech perception*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11020`; Keller et al. (2012), *Sensorimotor mismatch signals in primary visual cortex of the behaving mouse*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.040`.

title: Active touch sampling strategies
subfield: Touch, proprioception, vestibular processing, and multisensory integration
open: Explain how exploratory hand or whisker movements are selected to identify shape, texture, or compliance with minimal time and effort.
status: Mechanotransduction mechanisms and motor population dynamics provide components, but not an integrated tactile information-acquisition policy.
why: Connects perception to purposeful movement.
key_works: Ranade et al. (2014), *Piezo2 is the major transducer of mechanical forces for touch sensation in mice*, DOI: `10.1038/nature13980`; Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`.

title: Generalizable chronic-pain state biomarkers
open: Develop neural markers that predict clinically meaningful pain states across days and patients while separating pain from movement, mood, attention, and treatment effects.
status: Intracranial recordings predicted chronic pain states in a small human study in 2023; this is not a universal or context-free pain meter.
why: Enables better trials and adaptive treatment without replacing patient reports.
key_works: Shirvalkar et al. (2023), *First-in-human prediction of chronic pain state using intracranial neural biomarkers*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01338-z`.

title: Mechanistic transition from acute to chronic pain
open: Identify which changes make pain persist after an initiating injury and prospectively predict that transition before chronic pain is established.
status: Chronic-state biomarkers provide observations of established pain; they do not identify the causal transition or a universally preventive intervention.
why: Shifts treatment toward prevention of persistence.
key_works: Shirvalkar et al. (2023), *First-in-human prediction of chronic pain state using intracranial neural biomarkers*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01338-z`.

title: Causal control of pain without broad cognitive suppression
open: Use a validated individual pain-state model to suppress pathological pain while preserving protective sensation, cognition, and voluntary behavior.
status: Neural pain decoding supplies a possible feedback signal; successful decoding does not demonstrate safe causal control.
why: Creates a stringent target for closed-loop analgesia.
key_works: Shirvalkar et al. (2023), *First-in-human prediction of chronic pain state using intracranial neural biomarkers*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01338-z`; Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`.

title: Circuit code separating itch and pain
open: Determine how peripheral and spinal activity produces itch, pain, or mixed sensations, including the effects of stimulus intensity and chronic sensitization.
status: Gastrin-releasing-peptide-receptor circuitry supplies an important mechanistic foothold; it does not settle all labeled-line versus population-code questions.
why: Could produce treatments that suppress pathological itch without impairing protective sensation.
key_works: Sun and Chen (2007), *A gastrin-releasing peptide receptor mediates the itch sensation in the spinal cord*, DOI: `10.1038/nature06029`; Pagani et al. (2019), *How Gastrin-Releasing Peptide Opens the Spinal Gate for Itch* (verify bibliographic identifier).

title: Nociception-to-experienced-pain mapping
open: Explain when nociceptive activity becomes conscious pain and how expectations, attention, affect, and unconscious states change that relationship.
status: Pain-state prediction and consciousness measurements address different parts of the problem; neither identifies a universal mapping from tissue threat to experience.
why: Clarifies pain in noncommunicating patients and separates nociception from suffering.
key_works: Shirvalkar et al. (2023), *First-in-human prediction of chronic pain state using intracranial neural biomarkers*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01338-z`; Casali et al. (2013), *A theoretically based index of consciousness independent of sensory processing and behavior*, DOI: `10.1126/scitranslmed.3006294`.

title: Motor cortical dynamics-to-muscle commands
open: Determine which dimensions of motor population activity causally generate muscle activation and which reflect preparation, feedback, or correlated internal state.
status: Rotational population dynamics were demonstrated during reaching in 2012; descriptive dynamics do not by themselves identify the output-generating mechanism.
why: Connects population models to physical movement.
key_works: Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`; Michaels, Dann, and Scherberger (2016), *Neural Population Dynamics during Reaching Are Better Explained by a Dynamical System than Representational Tuning*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005175`.

title: Distributed action selection
open: Determine how competing actions are selected across basal ganglia, cortex, and brainstem without assigning selection to whichever region happens to encode the upcoming choice.
status: Brain-wide recordings reveal widespread behavioral variables, making causal allocation of selection functions more important rather than less.
why: Explains initiation, inhibition, and pathological action competition.
key_works: International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`.

title: Internal models of changing body mechanics
open: Identify how neural circuits estimate and update the mechanical properties of the body and external tools, and distinguish predictive models from learned feedback policies.
status: Motor dynamics and cerebellar learning findings support several computational descriptions; they do not uniquely identify the representation of body physics.
why: Explains rapid adaptation to loads, injuries, and tools.
key_works: Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`; Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`.

title: Fast acquisition of new motor skills
open: Determine how rapid changes in neural activity combine with slower synaptic and myelin changes to produce transferable motor skill.
status: Cortical dynamics and causal myelination experiments establish contributions on different timescales; their division of labor remains unresolved.
why: Guides rehabilitation schedules and skill-training methods.
key_works: Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`; McKenzie et al. (2014), *Motor skill learning requires active central myelination*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1254960`.

title: Flexible control through spinal circuitry
open: Determine the minimal descending information needed for spinal circuits to generate adaptable movement across terrains and body states.
status: A brain–spine interface enabled walking after spinal cord injury in a 2023 demonstration; the general spinal control code remains open.
why: Could simplify restorative interfaces and reveal natural control hierarchies.
key_works: Lorach et al. (2023), *Walking naturally after spinal cord injury using a brain–spine interface*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06094-5`.

title: What climbing-fiber signals teach
open: Determine when climbing-fiber activity conveys sensory error, reward, prediction, salience, or combinations, and derive the resulting plasticity rule.
status: Reward-related cerebellar signals challenge an exclusively motor-error description; the appropriate task-dependent teaching code remains unsettled.
why: Defines the learning objective of cerebellar circuits.
key_works: Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`; Larry et al. (2019), *Cerebellar climbing fibers encode expected reward size* (verify bibliographic identifier).

title: Granule-cell expansion recoding in natural tasks
open: Determine what representations granule cells construct from mossy-fiber input and whether expansion improves separability, temporal prediction, or another computational objective.
status: Reward-expectation coding demonstrates richer granule-cell signals than a purely static sensory expansion; the general transformation remains unresolved.
why: Tests central assumptions of cerebellar learning theories.
key_works: Marr (1969), *A theory of cerebellar cortex*, DOI: `10.1113/jphysiol.1969.sp008820`; Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`.

title: Common cerebellar algorithm across motor and cognitive tasks
open: Determine whether repeated cerebellar microcircuit architecture implements one reusable computation or several region-specific algorithms.
status: Reward-related activity and cerebellar influence on reward circuitry broaden the functional scope beyond motor coordination, without proving algorithmic uniformity.
why: Connects anatomical repetition to computational reuse.
key_works: Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`; Carta et al. (2019), *Cerebellar modulation of the reward circuitry and social behavior*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aav0581`.

title: Biological timing across milliseconds and seconds
open: Explain how cerebellar and connected circuits learn precise intervals over different timescales without assuming an unmeasured universal clock.
status: Classical cerebellar learning theories and modern reward-related recordings constrain possible timing mechanisms, but do not establish one cross-timescale solution.
why: Explains temporal coordination in movement, prediction, and cognition.
key_works: Marr (1969), *A theory of cerebellar cortex*, DOI: `10.1113/jphysiol.1969.sp008820`; Albus (1971), *A theory of cerebellar function*, DOI: `10.1016/0025-5564(71)90051-4`; Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`.

title: Cerebellar credit assignment for delayed outcomes
open: Identify how cerebellar plasticity associates an outcome with the relevant earlier activity when delays exceed a simple coincidence window.
status: Reward expectations are represented in cerebellar circuits; the temporal eligibility mechanism linking them to particular synapses remains a separate question.
why: Explains learning in temporally extended real-world actions.
key_works: Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`; Bellec et al. (2020), *A solution to the learning dilemma for recurrent networks of spiking neurons*, DOI: `10.1038/s41467-020-17236-y`.

title: Causal implementation of grid-cell attractors
open: Determine which connectivity and dynamics generate grid-cell population topology, and predict its deformation under targeted perturbations.
status: Toroidal population topology was demonstrated in 2022; observing a torus does not uniquely identify the circuit that generates it.
why: Connects a striking population geometry to a mechanistic navigation algorithm.
key_works: Gardner et al. (2022), *Toroidal topology of population activity in grid cells*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-021-04268-7`.

title: Navigation in complex three-dimensional spaces
open: Determine how spatial codes represent volumetric, vertically connected, deformable, or non-Euclidean environments, and how those representations support planning.
status: Toroidal grid-population results constrain familiar navigation settings but do not settle coding in arbitrary three-dimensional geometry.
why: Extends navigation theory beyond simplified flat arenas.
key_works: Gardner et al. (2022), *Toroidal topology of population activity in grid cells*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-021-04268-7`.

title: Joining local maps into global knowledge
open: Explain how separately learned spatial representations are aligned when an animal discovers a connection between environments, including inconsistent or ambiguous correspondences.
status: Place-code dynamics demonstrate representational flexibility, but do not specify a general map-merging algorithm.
why: Explains flexible route planning and discovery of shortcuts.
key_works: Ziv et al. (2013), *Long-term dynamics of CA1 hippocampal place codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3329`; Gardner et al. (2022), *Toroidal topology of population activity in grid cells*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-021-04268-7`.

title: Shared mechanisms for spatial and abstract maps
open: Determine whether spatial and nonspatial relational representations use the same learning and inference mechanisms or merely similar activity patterns.
status: Spatial population topology offers a strong mechanistic reference point; similarity to abstract representations does not establish computational identity.
why: Tests whether navigation circuitry supplies a reusable engine for relational thought.
key_works: Gardner et al. (2022), *Toroidal topology of population activity in grid cells*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-021-04268-7`; Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`.

title: Anchoring maps despite representational drift
open: Determine how stable landmarks, self-motion, and memory keep spatial behavior accurate while the participating neural ensemble changes.
status: Longitudinal CA1 recordings established substantial code dynamics; the anchor and readout mechanisms remain to be identified.
why: Explains reliable navigation over long periods.
key_works: Ziv et al. (2013), *Long-term dynamics of CA1 hippocampal place codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3329`.

title: Reading the content of an engram
open: Determine which features of an engram encode particular remembered content, rather than merely the probability of expressing a learned response.
status: Optogenetic activation of a hippocampal ensemble induced fear-memory recall in 2012; this does not reveal a complete content code.
why: Moves from locating memory-associated cells to understanding stored information.
key_works: Liu et al. (2012), *Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11028`.

title: Mechanism of systems consolidation
open: Determine how hippocampal and cortical contributions to a specific memory change over time, including whether information is copied, transformed, redistributed, or reconstructed.
status: Engram manipulation and longitudinal hippocampal recordings supply complementary evidence, but neither establishes a complete transfer algorithm.
why: Explains long-term retention and the effects of injury at different memory ages.
key_works: Liu et al. (2012), *Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11028`; Ziv et al. (2013), *Long-term dynamics of CA1 hippocampal place codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3329`.

title: Selective memory updating without collateral change
open: Modify one memory association while preserving related memories, factual content, and adaptive learning. Establish when retrieval permits updating and when it does not.
status: Engram activation provides selective access to some memory-associated ensembles, but access is not equivalent to precise, durable editing of one association.
why: Defines a stringent target for treating maladaptive memories.
key_works: Liu et al. (2012), *Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11028`; Frey and Morris (1997), *Synaptic tagging and long-term potentiation*, DOI: `10.1038/385533a0`.

title: Which substrate preserves very old memories
open: Determine the relative necessity of synaptic weights, connectivity, intrinsic excitability, and molecular states for retaining specific memories over long intervals.
status: Synaptic consolidation models explain possible persistence, while ensemble manipulations identify relevant cells; neither uniquely identifies the enduring substrate.
why: Distinguishes storage failure from retrieval failure.
key_works: Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`; Liu et al. (2012), *Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11028`.

title: Interference-resistant episodic storage
open: Explain how overlapping experiences remain distinguishable while still supporting generalization, and derive capacity limits under biologically realistic learning.
status: Multiscale memory models address retention, but retention alone does not settle interference between structured, overlapping episodes.
why: Connects memory capacity, abstraction, and forgetting.
key_works: Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`; Bittner et al. (2017), *Behavioral time scale synaptic plasticity underlies CA1 place fields*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aan3846`.

title: Mechanism of activity-silent working memory
subfield: Working memory, attention, and executive control
open: Determine whether apparently silent memories persist in synaptic changes, unobserved spiking, other cellular states, or combinations. Use measurements and perturbations that discriminate these alternatives.
status: TMS reactivated latent working-memory representations in 2016; reactivation does not uniquely identify the hidden storage substrate.
why: Resolves what persists between observable bursts of activity.
key_works: Rose et al. (2016), *Reactivation of latent working memories with transcranial magnetic stimulation*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aah7011`.

title: Mechanistic limits on working-memory capacity
subfield: Working memory, attention, and executive control
open: Derive task-dependent capacity and precision limits from neural mechanisms, including interference, attention, resource allocation, and representational similarity.
status: Latent-state reactivation expands candidate mechanisms beyond persistent firing, but does not settle capacity limits.
why: Explains why capacity changes with content and task.
