key_works: Rose et al. (2016), *Reactivation of latent working memories with transcranial magnetic stimulation*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aah7011`; Moreno-Bote et al. (2014), *Information-limiting correlations*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3807`.

title: Causal mechanism of attentional competition
subfield: Working memory, attention, and executive control
open: Identify how competing representations are enhanced or suppressed and how that competition is controlled across sensory modalities.
status: Attended-speaker representations demonstrate selective processing, but do not alone distinguish gain changes, routing, recurrent competition, or altered readout.
why: Explains selective access without assuming a single attention center.
key_works: Mesgarani and Chang (2012), *Selective cortical representation of attended speaker in multi-talker speech perception*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11020`; International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`.

title: Compositional executive control
subfield: Working memory, attention, and executive control
open: Explain how familiar rules and operations are recombined to solve a novel task without learning every combination separately.
status: Brain-wide task-variable representations and language-model alignment provide relevant observations, but not a verified neural algorithm for compositional control.
why: Addresses flexible reasoning rather than repeated task execution.
key_works: International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`; Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`.

title: Confidence versus decision evidence
subfield: Working memory, attention, and executive control
open: Determine how circuits distinguish confidence in a decision from the evidence, value, and motor preparation that accompany it.
status: Brain-wide prior-information representations reveal relevant signals, but shared correlations do not identify a separate metacognitive computation.
why: Explains calibrated self-evaluation and its failures.
key_works: Findling et al. (2025), *Brain-wide representations of prior information in mouse decision-making*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09226-1`.

title: Dopamine’s task-dependent teaching signals
open: Determine which dopamine signals instruct learning, which reflect movement or motivation, and how postsynaptic circuits interpret mixed signals.
status: Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation were demonstrated in 2019; this argues against treating every dopamine fluctuation as one universal scalar error.
why: Improves models of reward learning and dysfunction.
key_works: Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`.

title: Local control of dopamine release
open: Explain when terminal dopamine release diverges from source-neuron firing and determine how local circuit state changes its behavioral consequences.
status: The 2019 dissociation between dopamine dynamics related to learning and motivation highlights the importance of distinguishing somatic activity from local release.
why: Makes neuromodulatory measurements interpretable at the site of action.
key_works: Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`.

title: Arbitration between planning and cached habits
open: Determine how the brain chooses between explicit prospective evaluation and previously learned action values, including the costs of computation.
status: Distributed prior and decision signals provide potential substrates, but observing those signals does not identify an arbitration algorithm.
why: Explains flexibility, habits, and overreliance on costly deliberation.
key_works: Findling et al. (2025), *Brain-wide representations of prior information in mouse decision-making*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09226-1`; International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`.

title: Directed exploration versus behavioral noise
open: Identify neural mechanisms that distinguish purposeful information seeking from random variability, and predict exploration under novel uncertainty structures.
status: Large decision datasets expose trial-to-trial variability and prior effects, but these are not sufficient to identify the objective behind exploration.
why: Explains learning when rewards and world structure are initially unknown.
key_works: Findling et al. (2025), *Brain-wide representations of prior information in mouse decision-making*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09226-1`; Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`.

title: Physiological-state-dependent value
open: Explain how thirst, hunger, fatigue, and other bodily states transform the value of outcomes and the willingness to work for them.
status: Thirst circuits can anticipate physiological consequences, and dopamine signals distinguish aspects of motivation; a unified state-to-value computation remains open.
why: Connects homeostasis to flexible decision-making.
key_works: Zimmerman et al. (2016), *Thirst neurons anticipate the homeostatic consequences of eating and drinking*, DOI: `10.1038/nature18950`; Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`.

title: Neural implementation of compositional meaning
open: Determine how circuits combine word meanings and relations into novel sentence meanings, including counterfactual and structurally ambiguous cases.
status: Semantic maps and predictive language models explain important response variance; neither alone establishes the causal composition algorithm.
why: Explains understanding of sentences never previously encountered.
key_works: Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`; Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`.

title: Grounding linguistic concepts in perception and action
open: Identify how a concept’s linguistic, sensory, motor, and relational components interact, and determine which components are necessary in different contexts.
status: Natural-language imaging reveals distributed semantic organization, but a semantic response map is not a complete causal grounding model.
why: Explains meaning beyond text-to-text association.
key_works: Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`.

title: Cross-language neural representation alignment
open: Determine which neural representations are shared across languages and which depend on learned grammar, writing system, proficiency, or age of acquisition.
status: Strong language-encoding models provide a benchmark, but success on particular languages does not establish language-independent mechanisms.
why: Prevents language-specific samples from being mistaken for universal language neuroscience.
key_works: Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`; Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`.

title: Language-specific versus general reasoning computations
open: Distinguish neural computations needed for linguistic formulation from those needed for the underlying inference, using matched nonverbal tasks and causal perturbations.
status: Predictive language models can align with neural responses, but that alignment does not establish that language and thought use identical mechanisms.
why: Clarifies what language models can and cannot explain about cognition.
key_works: Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`.

title: Developmental emergence of language circuitry
open: Explain how genetic constraints, social interaction, perception, and learning jointly produce language-selective circuitry from early development.
status: Adult semantic maps and model alignment describe mature endpoints; they do not uniquely determine the developmental learning process.
why: Connects developmental biology, learning, and linguistic competence.
key_works: Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`; Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`.

title: Neural organization of emotional states
open: Determine whether emotional states are best explained by discrete circuit categories, continuous dimensions, context-dependent constructions, or a combination that predicts interventions.
status: Personalized closed-loop depression work demonstrates useful state-linked signals, but a clinically useful signal is not a universal taxonomy of emotion.
why: Establishes what mechanistic units emotion research should compare.
key_works: Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`.

title: Redundant mechanisms of social attachment
open: Determine how attachment persists when a proposed signaling pathway is absent, distinguishing developmental compensation, redundant circuitry, and context-dependent necessity.
status: Oxytocin-receptor knockout prairie voles retained social attachment in a 2023 study, challenging simple claims of universal receptor necessity.
why: Prevents overgeneralizing a single molecule into a complete social mechanism.
key_works: Berendzen et al. (2023), *Oxytocin receptor is not required for social attachment in prairie voles*, Neuron; PMID: `36708707`.

title: Inferring another individual’s hidden state
open: Identify how neural circuits infer another individual’s goals, beliefs, or feelings and distinguish genuine state inference from learned stimulus-response associations.
status: Social attachment and reward-circuit studies identify relevant mechanisms, but do not settle the computational basis of social inference.
why: Explains flexible social behavior in novel situations.
key_works: Berendzen et al. (2023), *Oxytocin receptor is not required for social attachment in prairie voles*, PMID: `36708707`; Carta et al. (2019), *Cerebellar modulation of the reward circuitry and social behavior*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aav0581`.

title: Causal interpretation of interacting-brain synchrony
open: Determine which apparent between-brain couplings reflect information exchange rather than shared sensory input, synchronized movement, or analysis artifacts.
status: Large-scale recording and reproducibility work sharpen the methodological problem; correlation between brains cannot by itself identify interpersonal causation.
why: Makes hyperscanning claims testable and mechanistically interpretable.
key_works: International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`; Botvinik-Nezer et al. (2020), *Variability in the analysis of a single neuroimaging dataset by many teams*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-020-2314-9`.

title: Generalization of safety learning
open: Determine why learned safety often remains context-specific and how to promote appropriate generalization without eliminating useful threat discrimination.
status: Selective memory-ensemble access and reopened social-learning windows provide possible experimental tools, not a complete solution to generalizing safety.
why: Addresses relapse of maladaptive fear outside treatment contexts.
key_works: Liu et al. (2012), *Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11028`; Nardou et al. (2023), *Psychedelics reopen the social reward learning critical period*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06204-3`.

title: Experiments that discriminate major consciousness theories
open: Specify predictions on which competing theories disagree, then test them with preregistered measurements that cannot be accommodated by changing the theory after seeing results.
status: The 2025 adversarial collaboration tested global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories, supporting and challenging different predictions rather than simply declaring one theory solved.
why: Converts broad frameworks into cumulative, falsifiable science.
key_works: Cogitate Consortium et al. (2025), *Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08888-1`; Melloni et al. (2023), *An adversarial collaboration protocol for testing contrasting predictions of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theory*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pone.0268577`.

title: Minimal sufficient neural substrate for a conscious content
open: Identify a neural mechanism sufficient for a particular conscious content while separating enabling conditions, reporting, attention, and downstream consequences.
status: Multimodal theory tests constrain candidate locations and dynamics, but correlates and task-related activation do not establish minimal sufficiency.
why: Moves beyond locating activity associated with awareness.
key_works: Cogitate Consortium et al. (2025), *Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08888-1`.

title: Consciousness measurement without report confounds
open: Validate measures of conscious state and content that do not require the very linguistic, attentional, or motor processes being distinguished from consciousness.
status: Perturbational complexity and dream-related cortical measurements provide partial approaches; neither supplies a universal content-sensitive, report-independent measure.
why: Enables work with infants, noncommunicating patients, and nonhuman animals.
key_works: Casali et al. (2013), *A theoretically based index of consciousness independent of sensory processing and behavior*, DOI: `10.1126/scitranslmed.3006294`; Siclari et al. (2017), *The neural correlates of dreaming*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4545`.

title: Reliable detection of covert consciousness
open: Detect preserved awareness in behaviorally unresponsive people with calibrated false-negative rates, repeatable bedside methods, and validated clinical consequences.
status: A 2024 multicenter study detected cognitive motor dissociation in a substantial subset of behaviorally unresponsive participants; negative tests still cannot be interpreted as simple proof of absent awareness.
why: Affects communication access, rehabilitation, and major clinical decisions.
key_works: Bodien et al. (2024), *Cognitive Motor Dissociation in Disorders of Consciousness*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2400645`.

title: Explanatory bridge from mechanism to experience
open: Develop an account that explains why specified physical processes correspond to particular experiences, while making clear which parts are empirical predictions and which are philosophical commitments.
status: The modern “hard problem” formulation dates to 1995. Formal theories and empirical comparisons have advanced, but no generally accepted explanatory bridge follows merely from locating neural correlates.
why: Clarifies what a complete theory of consciousness is claiming to explain.
key_works: Chalmers (1995), *Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness*, Journal of Consciousness Studies 2(3), 200–219; Albantakis et al. (2023), *Integrated information theory (IIT) 4.0: formulating the properties of phenomenal existence in physical terms*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011465`.

title: Cellular variables that generate sleep need
open: Identify the quantities accumulated during wakefulness that causally generate sleep pressure, and determine whether different cell populations track different needs.
status: Clearance and vascular studies establish processes linked to sleep, but none alone establishes the complete variable that makes sleep necessary.
why: Distinguishes causes of sleep need from processes that happen during sleep.
key_works: Xie et al. (2013), *Sleep drives metabolite clearance from the adult brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1241224`; Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`.

title: Functions of dreaming
open: Determine which consequences of dreaming depend on experienced dream content rather than on the underlying sleep physiology alone.
status: Neural correlates of dreaming were characterized in 2017; identifying when dreams occur does not establish why they occur.
why: Separates adaptive function, by-product, and subjective interpretation.
key_works: Siclari et al. (2017), *The neural correlates of dreaming*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4545`.

title: Selective memory consolidation during sleep
open: Explain which experiences are replayed or transformed during sleep, what selects them, and how those processes improve later behavior.
status: Memory-consolidation models and sleep-state measurements provide components, but not a complete selection policy for individual memories.
why: Explains why sleep strengthens some information while weakening or restructuring other information.
key_works: Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`; Siclari et al. (2017), *The neural correlates of dreaming*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4545`.

title: Distinct computational roles of REM and non-REM sleep
open: Determine which learning or maintenance operations require particular sleep states and whether their ordering matters causally.
status: Dreaming is not confined to a single simple state classification, and clearance findings depend on specific sleep dynamics; these observations resist one-function-per-stage accounts.
why: Guides mechanistically targeted treatment of disrupted sleep architecture.
key_works: Siclari et al. (2017), *The neural correlates of dreaming*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4545`; Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`.

title: Coordination of local sleep pressure and global timing
open: Explain how local circuit needs interact with global sleep-state transitions and circadian timing to determine when particular regions become unavailable for waking computation.
status: Spatially specific dream correlates and sleep-related vascular dynamics show that whole-brain stage labels omit important local variation.
why: Links local dysfunction to global sleep regulation.
key_works: Siclari et al. (2017), *The neural correlates of dreaming*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4545`; Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`.

title: Predictive homeostatic control
open: Determine how the brain predicts future physiological consequences before blood chemistry or other regulated variables have changed.
status: Thirst-neuron activity anticipates consequences of eating and drinking, demonstrated in 2016; the general predictive-control algorithm remains unresolved.
why: Explains anticipatory regulation rather than simple reactive feedback.
key_works: Zimmerman et al. (2016), *Thirst neurons anticipate the homeostatic consequences of eating and drinking*, DOI: `10.1038/nature18950`.

title: Vagal afferent population code
open: Determine how vagal populations encode combinations of mechanical, chemical, immune, and nutritional conditions, and how the brain disambiguates overlapping signals.
status: A defined gut nutrient-transduction circuit was demonstrated in 2018; one pathway does not establish a complete visceral sensory code.
why: Enables more selective interpretation and stimulation of visceral pathways.
key_works: Kaelberer et al. (2018), *A gut-brain neural circuit for nutrient sensory transduction*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5236`.

title: Bodily signals in affective experience
open: Quantify when interoceptive signals causally change emotion, when emotions alter bodily interpretation, and how the two directions interact.
status: Anticipatory homeostatic circuits and individualized mood-linked neural signals provide entry points, but not a complete bidirectional causal model.
why: Connects physiological regulation to anxiety, mood, and subjective feeling.
key_works: Zimmerman et al. (2016), *Thirst neurons anticipate the homeostatic consequences of eating and drinking*, DOI: `10.1038/nature18950`; Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`.

title: Multiobjective autonomic coordination
open: Explain how the nervous system coordinates cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, and thermoregulatory demands when improving one variable worsens another.
status: Specific anticipatory control pathways are known, but a general circuit-level account of tradeoffs across bodily systems remains open.
why: Explains coordinated physiology under exercise, stress, illness, and recovery.
key_works: Zimmerman et al. (2016), *Thirst neurons anticipate the homeostatic consequences of eating and drinking*, DOI: `10.1038/nature18950`; Kaelberer et al. (2018), *A gut-brain neural circuit for nutrient sensory transduction*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5236`.

title: Hormonal state-to-circuit reconfiguration
open: Determine how changing endocrine states reconfigure neural computations over hours to months, separating direct receptor effects from altered bodily and social experience.
status: Long-lasting pregnancy-associated brain-structure changes were reported in 2017; structural change does not specify its cellular mechanism or functional meaning.
why: Explains adaptive and pathological neural changes across major endocrine transitions.
key_works: Hoekzema et al. (2017), *Pregnancy leads to long-lasting changes in human brain structure*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4458`.

title: Enteric wiring-to-motility prediction
open: Predict gastrointestinal motor patterns from identified enteric cell types, connectivity, and local sensory inputs, including perturbation responses.
status: Human and mouse enteric single-cell atlases were published in 2020; a cell census is not a functional motility model.
why: Connects enteric classification to digestive function and dysfunction.
key_works: Drokhlyansky et al. (2020), *The Human and Mouse Enteric Nervous System at Single-Cell Resolution*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2020.08.003`.

title: Causal microbiome-to-neural pathways
open: Identify specific microbial products and host pathways that causally alter defined neural functions, separating neural, immune, endocrine, and dietary mediation.
status: Direct gut nutrient-transduction mechanisms provide a tractable route, but do not establish the many broader causal claims made about microbiome–brain relationships.
why: Converts broad associations into reproducible interventions.
key_works: Kaelberer et al. (2018), *A gut-brain neural circuit for nutrient sensory transduction*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5236`; Drokhlyansky et al. (2020), *The Human and Mouse Enteric Nervous System at Single-Cell Resolution*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2020.08.003`.

title: Human enteric functional diversity
open: Determine which molecularly defined human enteric populations perform distinct sensory, motor, and secretory functions and how those functions vary along the gut.
status: The 2020 atlas identifies candidate populations; direct human functional assignments remain a separate experimental program.
why: Enables cell-selective treatment rather than broad modulation of gut activity.
key_works: Drokhlyansky et al. (2020), *The Human and Mouse Enteric Nervous System at Single-Cell Resolution*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2020.08.003`.

title: Target-accurate peripheral reinnervation
open: Restore injured sensory or motor axons to appropriate targets with correct modality and timing, and quantify the limits imposed by target distance and chronic denervation.
status: Human mechanosensory deficits and neural-interface demonstrations clarify the required functions; anatomical regrowth alone would not establish correct reconnection.
why: Addresses functional failures after nerve injury.
key_works: Chesler et al. (2016), *The Role of PIEZO2 in Human Mechanosensation*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1602812`; Lorach et al. (2023), *Walking naturally after spinal cord injury using a brain–spine interface*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06094-5`.

title: Longitudinal enteric disease biomarkers
open: Develop minimally invasive measurements that track specific enteric neuronal or glial dysfunction before irreversible tissue damage, and validate them against physiological outcomes.
status: Molecular enteric reference maps provide candidate markers but not a validated longitudinal disease assay.
why: Makes the enteric nervous system accessible to earlier diagnosis and treatment monitoring.
key_works: Drokhlyansky et al. (2020), *The Human and Mouse Enteric Nervous System at Single-Cell Resolution*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2020.08.003`.

title: Avian–mammalian computational homology
open: Determine which bird and mammal forebrain computations derive from shared ancestral circuitry and which are convergent solutions implemented differently.
status: A cortex-like avian canonical circuit was described in 2020; architectural resemblance does not by itself settle evolutionary or computational identity.
why: Tests whether sophisticated cognition requires a particular cortical architecture.
key_works: Stacho et al. (2020), *A cortex-like canonical circuit in the avian forebrain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abc5534`.

title: Distributed control in cephalopod arms
open: Identify how local arm circuits and central brain signals coordinate flexible movement, sensory processing, and action selection.
status: The octopus genome revealed neural and morphological innovations in 2015; genomic information does not supply the distributed control algorithm.
why: Reveals alternatives to centralized control of highly deformable bodies.
key_works: Albertin et al. (2015), *The octopus genome and the evolution of cephalopod neural and morphological novelties*, DOI: `10.1038/nature14668`.

title: Computational consequences of neural RNA editing
open: Determine which RNA-editing events causally alter neural computation and adaptive behavior, and which are neutral or compensatory.
status: Extensive recoding in squid neural transcripts was demonstrated in 2015; a catalog of edits does not establish their individual functional significance.
why: Tests a form of neural molecular flexibility beyond genomic sequence.
key_works: Alon et al. (2015), *The majority of transcripts in the squid nervous system are extensively recoded by A-to-I RNA editing*, DOI: `10.7554/eLife.05198`.

title: Complete magnetoreception mechanism
open: Identify the in-vivo receptor, physical transduction process, neural pathway, and behavioral readout responsible for magnetic orientation in a defined species.
status: Migratory-songbird cryptochrome 4 showed magnetic sensitivity in 2021 experiments; this is not a complete receptor-to-navigation causal chain.
why: Would connect a subtle physical effect to a verified sensory system.
key_works: Xu et al. (2021), *Magnetic sensitivity of cryptochrome 4 from a migratory songbird*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-021-03618-9`.

title: Minimal circuits for flexible behavior
open: Determine the smallest neural systems capable of specified forms of learning, planning, or context-sensitive action, using explicit behavioral criteria and mechanistic models.
status: Worm-wide signal-propagation measurements offer an unusually constrained experimental system, but do not establish general minimality bounds.
why: Identifies which computational capabilities require which circuit resources.
key_works: Randi et al. (2023), *Neural signal propagation atlas of Caenorhabditis elegans*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06683-4`.

title: Variant-to-functional-phenotype chains
open: For a defined neurodevelopmental variant, establish the sequence from molecular change through developmental circuit alteration to a specific functional phenotype.
status: Large autism exome studies identify developmental and functional gene contributions; association alone does not establish the full mechanism.
why: Supports targeted help for particular impairments rather than treating heterogeneous diagnoses as single mechanisms.
key_works: Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`.

title: Variable penetrance of neurodevelopmental variants
open: Predict why people carrying similar risk variants have different developmental outcomes, incorporating genetic background, mosaicism, environment, and compensation.
status: Exome studies establish risk associations across many genes, but do not explain individual penetrance with sufficient mechanistic precision.
why: Improves prognosis without treating genetic risk as destiny.
key_works: Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`; Lodato et al. (2015), *Somatic mutation in single human neurons tracks developmental and transcriptional history*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aab1785`.

title: Reversible versus developmentally fixed consequences
open: Determine which consequences of a developmental perturbation remain reversible at each life stage and which require rebuilding circuit structure.
status: Critical-period reopening in mice demonstrates one route to renewed plasticity; it does not establish reversibility of arbitrary developmental conditions.
why: Defines realistic intervention targets and timing.
key_works: Nardou et al. (2023), *Psychedelics reopen the social reward learning critical period*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06204-3`; Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`.

title: Mechanistic subgroups within developmental diagnoses
open: Identify reproducible groups defined by causal mechanisms and support needs, rather than assuming all people sharing a diagnosis have the same circuit abnormality.
status: Genetic heterogeneity and the large samples needed for reliable brain-wide associations make simple one-signature accounts inadequate as a research endpoint.
why: Enables more relevant trials and individualized support.
key_works: Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`; Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`.

title: Validity of human developmental disease models
open: Establish which organoid or transplanted-cell phenotypes predict patient-relevant developmental outcomes and which reflect culture conditions or missing interactions.
status: Organoids model aspects of microcephaly and transplanted organoids can mature and integrate, but neither achievement certifies general clinical validity.
why: Makes model selection and drug screening evidence-based.
key_works: Lancaster et al. (2013), *Cerebral organoids model human brain development and microcephaly*, DOI: `10.1038/nature12517`; Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`.

title: Mechanistic psychiatric dimensions
open: Identify neural and physiological dimensions that explain symptoms, functional impairment, and intervention responses more reliably than diagnostic labels alone.
status: Personalized depression stimulation and large-scale association studies provide complementary evidence, but neither establishes a universal mechanistic taxonomy.
why: Makes treatment development less dependent on heterogeneous categories.
key_works: Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`; Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`.

title: Prospective antidepressant-treatment selection
open: Predict which treatment will benefit an individual before prolonged trial and error, and validate the prediction in randomized treatment-selection studies.
status: A 2021 single-patient closed-loop demonstration established an important personalized intervention, not a broadly validated treatment-selection rule.
why: Reduces time spent receiving ineffective treatment.
key_works: Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`.

title: Schizophrenia risk genes to circuit computation
open: Determine how identified risk pathways alter specific operations such as inference, working memory, or sensory integration, and identify reversible mediators.
status: The 2022 genomic study implicates synaptic biology and many loci; it does not collapse schizophrenia into one circuit defect.
why: Connects genetic discovery to mechanistically targeted treatment.
key_works: Trubetskoy et al. (2022), *Mapping genomic loci implicates genes and synaptic biology in schizophrenia*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04434-5`.

title: Persistent relapse vulnerability in addiction
open: Identify which learned, motivational, and physiological states preserve relapse risk after prolonged abstinence, and selectively change them without broadly suppressing reward.
status: Distinct dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation provide a useful mechanistic separation, but do not establish a complete relapse model.
why: Targets persistence rather than only acute drug effects.
key_works: Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`; Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`.

title: Therapeutic plasticity versus nonspecific drug effects
open: Determine which treatment-induced plasticity changes are necessary for durable psychiatric benefit and how they interact with subsequent experience.
status: Psychedelic reopening of social-reward learning windows in mice is a mechanistic result, not proof that the same process explains all human therapeutic effects.
why: Separates candidate mechanisms from broad narratives about increased plasticity.
key_works: Nardou et al. (2023), *Psychedelics reopen the social reward learning critical period*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06204-3`.

title: Rate and function of adult human neurogenesis
open: Quantify neuron production, survival, integration, and functional contribution across adult human ages and conditions using convergent methods.
status: Proliferating neural progenitors in the adult human hippocampus were reported in 2025. The remaining target is not a blanket claim that adult progenitors have never been observed.
why: Determines the relevance of neurogenesis to aging and repair.
key_works: Dumitru et al. (2025), *Identification of proliferating neural progenitors in the adult human hippocampus*, DOI: `10.1126/science.adu9575`; Eriksson et al. (1998), *Neurogenesis in the adult human hippocampus*, DOI: `10.1038/3305`.

title: Mechanisms of cognitive resilience
open: Explain why some people retain function despite substantial pathology, separating compensatory circuitry, reserve, cell resistance, and measurement differences.
status: Amyloid-targeting trials establish that modifying one pathological process can affect decline, but they do not explain individual resilience to pathology.
why: Could reveal protective mechanisms complementary to pathology removal.
key_works: van Dyck et al. (2023), *Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer’s Disease*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2212948`; Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.

title: Amyloid reduction-to-clinical-benefit mechanism
open: Determine which downstream changes mediate benefit from amyloid reduction, why benefit varies, and which combinations are needed for substantially larger functional effects.
status: Lecanemab reduced decline relative to placebo in its pivotal trial; longer follow-up has been reported. Slowing decline is not equivalent to restoring lost function.
why: Guides treatment combinations and patient selection.
key_works: van Dyck et al. (2023), *Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer’s Disease*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2212948`; van Dyck et al. (2025), *Long-term safety and efficacy of lecanemab in early Alzheimer’s disease: Results from the clarity AD open-label extension study*, DOI: `10.1002/alz.70905`.

title: Toxic tau species and causal propagation
open: Identify which tau assemblies cause neuronal dysfunction, which mainly mark disease, and which processes are necessary for spread between cells.
status: Human Alzheimer tau filament structures were resolved in 2017; structural identification does not establish that every observed assembly has the same toxicity or propagation role.
why: Makes anti-tau interventions target the relevant species and processes.
key_works: Fitzpatrick et al. (2017), *Cryo-EM structures of tau filaments from Alzheimer’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/nature23002`.

title: Restoring function after established dementia-related loss
open: Restore clinically meaningful memory or daily function after substantial circuit damage, rather than only reducing future decline.
status: Disease-modifying amyloid trials establish partial slowing, while cell-integration studies provide separate repair tools; neither demonstrates general restoration of lost dementia-related function.
why: Addresses the gap between prevention of further damage and recovery.
key_works: van Dyck et al. (2023), *Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer’s Disease*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2212948`; Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`.

title: Durable benefit from dopaminergic cell replacement
open: Establish long-term, controlled clinical benefit from replacement dopamine neurons, including stable integration, appropriate regulation, and protection from recurrent pathology.
status: A 2025 phase I hES-derived dopaminergic-cell trial is an important milestone; early safety and feasibility do not settle durable comparative efficacy.
why: Tests whether cell replacement becomes a reproducible restorative treatment.
key_works: Tabar et al. (2025), *Phase I trial of hES cell-derived dopaminergic neurons for Parkinson’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08845-y`.

title: Parkinson’s mechanisms beyond dopamine replacement
open: Identify and treat the mechanisms responsible for major nonmotor and treatment-resistant manifestations, rather than assuming restoration of dopamine solves the entire disease.
status: Dopaminergic replacement trials target one important component; their scope does not establish correction of all affected circuits or cell types.
why: Addresses disability left outside dopamine-centered interventions.
key_works: Tabar et al. (2025), *Phase I trial of hES cell-derived dopaminergic neurons for Parkinson’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08845-y`; Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.

title: TDP-43 loss of function versus toxic gain of function
open: Quantify the contributions of nuclear depletion, altered RNA processing, cytoplasmic assemblies, and downstream stress to ALS and frontotemporal degeneration.
status: Pathological TDP-43 was identified in these diseases in 2006; identifying the protein did not settle which consequences are causally dominant.
why: Determines whether therapy should restore function, remove assemblies, or do both.
key_works: Neumann et al. (2006), *Ubiquitinated TDP-43 in frontotemporal lobar degeneration and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1134108`.

title: Biomarker improvement-to-functional benefit in ALS
open: Determine when molecular target engagement predicts meaningful motor and survival benefit, and identify optimal intervention timing for genetically defined ALS.
status: The 2022 tofersen trial separated biomarker effects from its primary short-term clinical endpoint; subsequent long-term work underscores the need for timing-sensitive interpretation.
why: Improves trial design and avoids equating molecular change with clinical recovery.
key_works: Miller et al. (2022), *Trial of Antisense Oligonucleotide Tofersen for SOD1 ALS*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2204705`; Miller et al. (2026), *Long-Term Tofersen in SOD1 Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis* (verify bibliographic identifier).

title: Selective neuronal vulnerability
open: Explain why particular neuronal populations fail in a proteinopathy while nearby cells exposed to similar pathology survive.
status: Molecular cell atlases and disease-protein structures provide candidate explanatory variables, but neither alone predicts selective death.
why: Could reveal protection mechanisms shared across degenerative diseases.
key_works: Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`; Fitzpatrick et al. (2017), *Cryo-EM structures of tau filaments from Alzheimer’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/nature23002`.

title: Reliable individual seizure forecasting
open: Forecast seizure risk with calibrated probabilities over clinically useful horizons across changing medication, sleep, and disease states.
status: Development and validation studies demonstrate forecasting potential; reliable long-term individual calibration and actionable warning policies remain separate targets.
why: Enables risk-aware daily planning and preventive intervention.
key_works: Proix et al. (2021), *Forecasting seizure risk in adults with focal epilepsy: a development and validation study*, DOI: `10.1016/S1474-4422(20)30396-3`.

title: Mechanisms that create an epileptic circuit
open: Identify which changes after injury or genetic perturbation are necessary for epileptogenesis and interrupt them before recurrent seizures become established.
status: Seizure-risk forecasting describes susceptibility dynamics but does not establish the causal developmental transition into epilepsy.
why: Distinguishes disease prevention from suppressing individual seizures.
key_works: Proix et al. (2021), *Forecasting seizure risk in adults with focal epilepsy: a development and validation study*, DOI: `10.1016/S1474-4422(20)30396-3`; Prinz, Bucher, and Marder (2004), *Similar network activity from disparate circuit parameters*, DOI: `10.1038/nn1352`.

title: Minimal interventions that terminate seizures
open: Determine the spatially and temporally minimal perturbations needed to terminate different seizure types while preserving normal function.
status: Risk forecasting and long-term neural recording improve observation, but a general, patient-specific control law for seizure termination remains open.
why: Reduces stimulation burden and unintended effects.
key_works: Proix et al. (2021), *Forecasting seizure risk in adults with focal epilepsy: a development and validation study*, DOI: `10.1016/S1474-4422(20)30396-3`; Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`.

title: Migraine attack initiation
open: Determine the causal sequence that initiates an attack in a particular person and distinguish initiating processes from symptoms or amplifying pathways.
status: CGRP-pathway prevention has demonstrated clinical efficacy; efficacy of a downstream intervention does not by itself identify the universal initiating event.
why: Supports prevention earlier in the attack-generating process.
key_works: Goadsby et al. (2017), *A Controlled Trial of Erenumab for Episodic Migraine*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1705848`.

title: Mechanism-based migraine treatment selection
open: Predict response and adverse effects for an individual across preventive treatment classes using validated mechanistic biomarkers.
status: Controlled erenumab trials establish group-level benefit, not a complete individualized treatment-selection rule.
why: Reduces repeated unsuccessful treatment trials.
key_works: Goadsby et al. (2017), *A Controlled Trial of Erenumab for Episodic Migraine*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1705848`.

title: Long-distance CNS axon regeneration with correct targets
open: Regrow injured central axons over clinically relevant distances, reconnect appropriate targets, and demonstrate useful, stable function without maladaptive sprouting.
status: Manipulating PTEN/mTOR promoted adult CNS axon regeneration in 2008; growth promotion alone does not solve target selection and integration.
why: Addresses a core barrier to repairing severed central pathways.
key_works: Park et al. (2008), *Promoting axon regeneration in the adult CNS by modulation of the PTEN/mTOR pathway*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1161566`.

title: Broad functional restoration after spinal cord injury
open: Restore coordinated mobility together with sensory and autonomic functions across diverse injuries, rather than demonstrating a single assisted motor task.
status: The 2023 brain–spine interface restored walking in a proof-of-concept setting; general recovery across people and functions remains open.
why: Targets the full burden of spinal injury.
key_works: Lorach et al. (2023), *Walking naturally after spinal cord injury using a brain–spine interface*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06094-5`.

title: Large, durable recovery in chronic stroke
open: Produce substantial functional recovery in chronic stroke across heterogeneous lesion locations, with transfer to daily activities and sustained benefit.
status: Paired vagus-nerve stimulation and rehabilitation improved upper-limb outcomes in a 2021 controlled trial; that does not establish broad restoration across stroke deficits.
why: Addresses disability after spontaneous recovery has slowed.
key_works: Dawson et al. (2021), *Vagus nerve stimulation paired with rehabilitation for upper limb motor function after ischaemic stroke (VNS-REHAB): a randomised, blinded, pivotal, device trial*, DOI: `10.1016/S0140-6736(21)00475-X`.

title: Mechanistic prognosis after diffuse brain injury
open: Predict recovery from distributed injury using measurements that separate damaged pathways, reversible dysfunction, preserved awareness, and capacity for compensation.
status: Multicenter detection of cognitive motor dissociation shows that behavioral unresponsiveness can conceal preserved processing; this complicates simple prognostic labels.
why: Improves rehabilitation allocation and reduces premature certainty.
key_works: Bodien et al. (2024), *Cognitive Motor Dissociation in Disorders of Consciousness*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2400645`.

title: Repair without losing protective injury responses
open: Identify interventions that permit regeneration while preserving necessary wound containment, immune defense, and tissue stability.
status: Growth-promoting manipulations and protective microglial effects illustrate different requirements; maximizing growth alone is not a complete repair strategy.
why: Avoids exchanging one form of damage for another.
key_works: Park et al. (2008), *Promoting axon regeneration in the adult CNS by modulation of the PTEN/mTOR pathway*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1161566`; Wheeler et al. (2018), *Microglia are required for protection against lethal coronavirus encephalitis in mice*, DOI: `10.1172/JCI97229`.

title: Selective disruption of neuron–glioma communication
open: Interrupt tumor-supporting neural interactions without broadly impairing normal synaptic transmission, and demonstrate improved clinical outcomes.
status: Glioma integration into neural circuits was demonstrated in 2019; identifying tumor-associated synapses is not yet equivalent to a selective effective therapy.
why: Targets a tumor-support mechanism distinct from autonomous cancer-cell growth.
key_works: Venkatesh et al. (2019), *Electrical and synaptic integration of glioma into neural circuits*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1563-y`; Venkataramani et al. (2019), *Glutamatergic synaptic input to glioma cells drives brain tumour progression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1564-x`.

title: Tumor-induced circuit remodeling
open: Determine how tumors change surrounding neural computation and which changes cause seizures, cognitive deficits, or further tumor growth.
status: Neuron–glioma electrical integration supplies a mechanism for bidirectional interaction, but not a complete model of surrounding circuit dysfunction.
why: Connects tumor biology to neurological symptoms and treatment priorities.
key_works: Venkatesh et al. (2019), *Electrical and synaptic integration of glioma into neural circuits*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1563-y`.

title: Clearing neural infection without immune-mediated injury
open: Identify treatment schedules that control a pathogen while preventing destructive inflammation and preserving necessary immune functions.
status: Microglial protection in experimental coronavirus encephalitis demonstrates that suppressing brain immunity indiscriminately can remove a beneficial mechanism.
why: Balances infection control and preservation of neural tissue.
key_works: Wheeler et al. (2018), *Microglia are required for protection against lethal coronavirus encephalitis in mice*, DOI: `10.1172/JCI97229`.

title: Persistent dysfunction after pathogen clearance
open: Determine whether lasting postinfectious symptoms result from residual pathogen, immune memory, vascular damage, synaptic loss, or other mechanisms in defined patient groups.
status: Acute neuroinfection studies establish protective immune responses, while EBV–MS evidence establishes a long-latency disease connection; neither supplies a universal postinfectious mechanism.
why: Prevents heterogeneous postinfectious states from being treated as one process.
key_works: Wheeler et al. (2018), *Microglia are required for protection against lethal coronavirus encephalitis in mice*, DOI: `10.1172/JCI97229`; Bjornevik et al. (2022), *Longitudinal analysis reveals high prevalence of Epstein-Barr virus associated with multiple sclerosis*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abj8222`.

title: Longitudinal tumor–neuron interaction atlas
open: Create matched longitudinal measurements of tumor genotype, cell state, neural connectivity, electrical activity, treatment, and clinical outcomes.
status: The 2019 neuron–glioma studies establish relevant interactions; a standardized longitudinal intervention-linked atlas is a further data target.
why: Enables prediction of tumor–circuit evolution and treatment escape.
key_works: Venkatesh et al. (2019), *Electrical and synaptic integration of glioma into neural circuits*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1563-y`; Venkataramani et al. (2019), *Glutamatergic synaptic input to glioma cells drives brain tumour progression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1564-x`.

title: Adult-like maturation of human neural organoids
subfield: Organoids, engineered tissue, and cell replacement
open: Produce organoids with validated adult-like molecular, electrophysiological, metabolic, and plasticity properties without equating one maturation marker with adulthood.
status: Organoids model aspects of development, and transplantation improves maturation and integration; fully validated adult-like equivalence remains a separate target.
why: Enables better models of adult disease and physiology.
key_works: Lancaster et al. (2013), *Cerebral organoids model human brain development and microcephaly*, DOI: `10.1038/nature12517`; Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`.

title: Perfused neural tissue with realistic support cells
subfield: Organoids, engineered tissue, and cell replacement
open: Build reproducible neural tissue with functional perfusion, barrier properties, immune components, and glial support at scales sufficient for sustained complex physiology.
status: Cerebral organoids and transplanted organoids provide partial systems, but combining all supporting compartments reproducibly is a distinct engineering problem.
why: Reduces artifacts caused by missing supply and support systems.
key_works: Lancaster et al. (2013), *Cerebral organoids model human brain development and microcephaly*, DOI: `10.1038/nature12517`; Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`.

title: Reproducible organoid assembly across laboratories
subfield: Organoids, engineered tissue, and cell replacement
open: Define manufacturing and acceptance criteria that predict composition, connectivity, and function across batches, donors, and laboratories.
status: Foundational organoid work establishes useful models, but model availability is not equivalent to interchangeability or standardized functional quality.
why: Makes screening and replication interpretable.
key_works: Lancaster et al. (2013), *Cerebral organoids model human brain development and microcephaly*, DOI: `10.1038/nature12517`; Botvinik-Nezer et al. (2020), *Variability in the analysis of a single neuroimaging dataset by many teams*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-020-2314-9`.

title: Target-specific integration of grafted neurons
subfield: Organoids, engineered tissue, and cell replacement
open: Ensure transplanted neurons receive appropriate inputs, project to intended targets, and improve the desired function without creating pathological activity.
status: Transplanted human cortical organoids can integrate with host circuits; integration itself does not guarantee task-appropriate connectivity or clinical benefit.
why: Makes cell replacement a circuit-repair strategy rather than simply cell survival.
key_works: Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`; Tabar et al. (2025), *Phase I trial of hES cell-derived dopaminergic neurons for Parkinson’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08845-y`.

title: Long-term safety assurance for neural grafts
subfield: Organoids, engineered tissue, and cell replacement
open: Establish sensitive, scalable methods to exclude dangerous residual cell states and detect later overgrowth, migration, immune incompatibility, or dysfunctional integration.
status: Early clinical cell-replacement trials establish a path to testing, but long-term safety requires evidence beyond initial tolerability.
why: Enables neural grafts to move from small trials to dependable treatment.
key_works: Tabar et al. (2025), *Phase I trial of hES cell-derived dopaminergic neurons for Parkinson’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08845-y`; Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`.

title: Years-long identity of individual recorded neurons
open: Track the same identified neurons over years with explicit confidence in identity, while separating true biological change from probe motion and recording instability.
status: Neuropixels 2.0 demonstrated substantially improved stable long-term recordings; that milestone is not equivalent to years-long verified identity in arbitrary conditions.
why: Enables rigorous studies of learning, aging, and disease progression.
key_works: Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`.

title: Simultaneous whole-brain cellular recording in behaving mammals
open: Record relevant fast activity across an entire mammalian brain simultaneously, with quantified coverage and perturbation of normal behavior.
status: The 2025 brain-wide mouse map aggregates extensive recordings across animals and sessions; it is not simultaneous cellular recording of one whole brain.
why: Resolves coordination that cannot be reconstructed reliably from separate sessions.
key_works: International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`; Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`.

title: Tenfold lower photon burden for voltage imaging
open: Reduce required illumination per accurately detected voltage event by at least tenfold against a specified baseline while maintaining temporal resolution, coverage, and biological safety.
status: Proposed moonshot. Chemigenetic voltage indicators such as Voltron improved brightness and photostability; the target must be assessed with end-to-end detection and toxicity measurements.
why: Extends recording duration and access to fragile tissue.
key_works: Abdelfattah et al. (2019), *Bright and photostable chemigenetic indicators for extended in vivo voltage imaging*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aav6416`.

title: Multiplexed fast chemical signaling measurements
open: Simultaneously measure multiple transmitters, peptides, ions, and metabolic variables at useful spatial and temporal resolution without substantial cross-talk or buffering artifacts.
status: Local dopamine measurements show why electrical activity alone is insufficient; a comprehensive multiplexed chemical readout remains a broader instrumentation target.
why: Makes neuromodulatory and metabolic circuit states observable.
key_works: Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`; Suzuki et al. (2011), *Astrocyte-neuron lactate transport is required for long-term memory formation*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2011.02.018`.

title: Reversible cell-type-specific perturbation in humans
open: Develop safe, reversible ways to manipulate defined human neural populations with sufficient specificity to test causal hypotheses and treat dysfunction.
status: Human neuromodulation and cell atlases advance intervention and targeting separately; their combination does not yet yield arbitrary cell-type-specific human control.
why: Bridges a major gap between animal causal experiments and human treatment.
key_works: Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`; Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.

title: Cellular interpretation of human hemodynamic imaging
subfield: MRI, MEG, EEG, and multiscale imaging
open: Infer which cellular activities produced a measured hemodynamic signal under different physiological states, with uncertainty that includes vascular and metabolic variation.
status: Neural energy budgets and sleep-related vascular mechanisms expose important non-neuronal determinants; they do not solve the inverse mapping.
why: Prevents overprecise neural claims from indirect measurements.
key_works: Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`; Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`.

title: Identifiability limits of EEG and MEG sources
subfield: MRI, MEG, EEG, and multiscale imaging
open: Derive realistic limits on which source configurations can be distinguished using practical sensors, anatomy, and noise, and determine which added measurements break ambiguities.
status: Wearable MEG improves measurement access, but sensor innovation does not eliminate the underlying inverse problem.
why: Establishes defensible spatial and mechanistic claims.
key_works: Boto et al. (2018), *Moving magnetoencephalography towards real-world applications with a wearable system*, DOI: `10.1038/nature26147`.

title: Tenfold cheaper practical MEG
subfield: MRI, MEG, EEG, and multiscale imaging
open: Reduce fully loaded cost of useful MEG acquisition by at least tenfold while maintaining preregistered sensitivity, localization performance, movement tolerance, and operational reliability.
status: Proposed moonshot. Wearable optically pumped magnetometer systems established an alternative measurement architecture in 2018; total-cost and deployment targets require separate verification.
why: Expands access beyond a small number of specialized facilities.
key_works: Boto et al. (2018), *Moving magnetoencephalography towards real-world applications with a wearable system*, DOI: `10.1038/nature26147`.

title: Same-subject multiscale brain measurements
subfield: MRI, MEG, EEG, and multiscale imaging
open: Align molecular, cellular, circuit, whole-brain, and behavioral measurements from the same individuals with explicit registration uncertainty.
status: MICrONS combines important functional and structural scales, while human atlases provide molecular breadth; comprehensive same-subject integration remains a larger target.
why: Prevents cross-scale explanations from depending entirely on unmatched populations.
key_works: MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`; Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.

title: Physical limits of noninvasive cellular-resolution recording
subfield: MRI, MEG, EEG, and multiscale imaging
open: Establish modality-specific lower bounds on resolution, depth, bandwidth, heating, and signal-to-noise for recording deep human neural activity noninvasively.
status: Wearable magnetic sensing and invasive high-density probes represent different tradeoffs; neither establishes the ultimate feasible noninvasive frontier.
why: Separates plausible moonshots from targets blocked by specified physical constraints.
key_works: Boto et al. (2018), *Moving magnetoencephalography towards real-world applications with a wearable system*, DOI: `10.1038/nature26147`; Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`.

title: Decade-scale stable neural interfaces
open: Maintain useful bidirectional neural-interface performance for a decade with manageable maintenance, no unacceptable tissue damage, and graceful recovery from component failure.
status: Long-term recording advances and successful speech interfaces establish important components; decade-scale dependable service is a separate systems target.
why: Makes implants practical lifelong tools rather than short research demonstrations.
key_works: Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`; Card et al. (2024), *An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2314132`.

title: Cross-user and cross-language neural decoding
open: Build decoders that transfer across users, languages, recording configurations, and changing impairments with minimal safe calibration.
status: High-performance and rapidly calibrating speech interfaces demonstrate major progress, but general transfer with validated failure detection remains a broader requirement.
why: Reduces setup burden and expands access.
key_works: Willett et al. (2023), *A high-performance speech neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06377-x`; Card et al. (2024), *An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2314132`.

title: Naturalistic continuous speech restoration
open: Restore low-latency conversational speech with reliable turn-taking, prosody, corrections, silence detection, and user control outside laboratory scripts.
status: Speech neuroprostheses and 2025 streaming brain-to-voice work establish substantial components; dependable unrestricted everyday conversation remains a systems-level target.
why: Measures success in actual communication rather than isolated decoding scores.
key_works: Willett et al. (2023), *A high-performance speech neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06377-x`; Littlejohn et al. (2025), *A streaming brain-to-voice neuroprosthesis to restore naturalistic communication*, PMID: `40164740`.

title: Biomimetic sensory feedback for prostheses
open: Deliver useful touch, position, and force feedback that supports dexterous control and feels interpretable without excessive training or interference.
status: PIEZO2 studies clarify natural mechanosensory requirements, while brain–spine interfaces demonstrate restorative control; replacing the corresponding rich feedback remains distinct.
why: Closes the loop between intended action and sensed outcome.
key_works: Chesler et al. (2016), *The Role of PIEZO2 in Human Mechanosensation*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1602812`; Lorach et al. (2023), *Walking naturally after spinal cord injury using a brain–spine interface*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06094-5`.

title: Distinguishing intended communication from private thought
open: Ensure a communication BCI emits only intentionally authorized output, with robust suppression of accidental activation and transparent user correction.
status: Speech-decoding successes make intention gating an important independent acceptance criterion; accuracy on instructed attempts does not establish privacy during unrestricted use.
why: Preserves agency and trust in assistive communication.
key_works: Card et al. (2024), *An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2314132`; UNESCO (2025), *Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology*.

title: Focal noninvasive stimulation of deep targets
open: Stimulate a specified deep target while minimizing effects on intervening and neighboring tissue, with independently verified target engagement.
status: Temporal interference was introduced experimentally in 2017 and investigated in the human hippocampus in 2023; general focality and mechanism remain active questions.
why: Could reduce the need for invasive access.
key_works: Grossman et al. (2017), *Noninvasive Deep Brain Stimulation via Temporally Interfering Electric Fields*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2017.05.024`; Violante et al. (2023), *Non-invasive temporal interference electrical stimulation of the human hippocampus*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01456-8`.

title: Patient-specific stimulation response models
open: Predict how stimulation parameters alter a patient’s circuit and symptoms, including adaptation, side effects, and changing disease state.
status: Personalized closed-loop depression treatment demonstrates a useful individual approach; generalizable response identification remains unresolved.
why: Replaces repeated empirical parameter search with predictive control.
key_works: Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`; Violante et al. (2023), *Non-invasive temporal interference electrical stimulation of the human hippocampus*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01456-8`.

title: Selective delivery to distributed neural cell populations
open: Deliver molecular therapies to the intended neural cell populations across clinically relevant tissue volumes while minimizing off-target expression and immune toxicity.
status: Human cell atlases improve target definition and antisense trials establish molecular intervention potential; precise broad delivery remains a separate bottleneck.
why: Determines whether molecularly precise therapies can reach their targets.
key_works: Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`; Miller et al. (2022), *Trial of Antisense Oligonucleotide Tofersen for SOD1 ALS*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2204705`.

title: Artifact-free simultaneous neural reading and writing
open: Measure relevant neural responses during stimulation with error bounds that distinguish biological effects from electrical, optical, and computational artifacts.
status: Closed-loop treatment and high-density recording demonstrate key components; simultaneous measurement fidelity remains an independent validation requirement.
why: Prevents control systems from reacting to their own artifacts.
key_works: Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`; Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`.

title: Safe autonomous home neuromodulation
open: Operate a therapeutic closed-loop system at home with bounded stimulation, drift detection, recoverable failures, patient override, and demonstrated clinical benefit.
status: Individual closed-loop demonstrations establish feasibility, not universal unattended reliability or long-term serviceability.
why: Converts laboratory neurotechnology into accessible ongoing care.
key_works: Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`; UNESCO (2025), *Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology*.

title: Minimum interventions for circuit identification
subfield: Causal inference and mechanistic theory evaluation
open: Determine the minimum number and diversity of interventions needed to identify a circuit’s causal dynamics under hidden inputs, partial observation, and measurement noise.
status: Circuit degeneracy establishes nonuniqueness from activity alone, while worm-wide perturbation maps show what richer interventions can reveal.
why: Makes causal experiments more efficient and their conclusions more defensible.
key_works: Prinz, Bucher, and Marder (2004), *Similar network activity from disparate circuit parameters*, DOI: `10.1038/nn1352`; Randi et al. (2023), *Neural signal propagation atlas of Caenorhabditis elegans*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06683-4`.

title: Interpreting perturbations that change many variables
subfield: Causal inference and mechanistic theory evaluation
open: Determine when a neural perturbation identifies the natural role of its target rather than inducing an unnatural network state, compensatory response, or off-target effect.
status: Known-system analysis demonstrated that standard neuroscience-style tools can produce incomplete explanations even when the entire system is available.
why: Improves the inference from “perturbation changes behavior” to mechanism.
key_works: Jonas and Kording (2017), *Could a neuroscientist understand a microprocessor?*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005268`.

title: Benchmarks for mechanistic understanding
subfield: Causal inference and mechanistic theory evaluation
open: Define tests that require models to predict unseen interventions, failures, and recovery—not merely correlate with recorded activity.
status: The microprocessor study supplies a cautionary known-ground-truth example; latent-variable benchmarks assess another useful but narrower capability.
why: Gives “understanding” an operational criterion.
key_works: Jonas and Kording (2017), *Could a neuroscientist understand a microprocessor?*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005268`; Pei et al. (2021), *Neural Latents Benchmark ’21: Evaluating latent variable models of neural population activity*, arXiv: `2109.04463`.

title: Transporting causal findings across individuals and species
subfield: Causal inference and mechanistic theory evaluation
open: Specify when a causal effect measured in one organism or context should transfer to another and identify the measurements needed to justify that transfer.
status: Comparative atlases and multicenter standardized experiments improve comparability, but similarity of labels or average responses is not a transportability proof.
why: Strengthens translation from model systems to human interventions.
key_works: Krienen et al. (2023), *A marmoset brain cell census reveals regional specialization of cellular identities*, DOI: `10.1126/sciadv.adk3986`; International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`.

title: Behavioral completeness for interpreting neural activity
subfield: Causal inference and mechanistic theory evaluation
open: Determine which unmeasured movements, strategies, internal states, and environmental variables materially confound a neural explanation, and establish sufficient behavioral measurement standards.
status: Brain-wide task maps reveal widespread behavioral signals; increasingly comprehensive neural recording does not compensate automatically for incomplete behavioral observation.
why: Prevents neural activity from being assigned to the wrong psychological process.
key_works: International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`; Jonas and Kording (2017), *Could a neuroscientist understand a microprocessor?*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005268`.

title: Interoperable whole-experiment records
open: Represent acquisition, behavioral events, interventions, calibration, anatomy, processing, and uncertainty in interoperable machine-readable records that preserve meaning across laboratories.
status: Neurodata Without Borders provides a substantial ecosystem; existing standards do not mean every experimental modality or semantic relationship is covered consistently.
why: Makes pooled analysis and independent reconstruction feasible.
key_works: Rübel et al. (2022), *The Neurodata Without Borders ecosystem for neurophysiological data science*, DOI: `10.7554/eLife.78362`.

title: Persistent identity across neural datasets
open: Maintain auditable identity links for subjects, samples, cells, recordings, anatomical reconstructions, and derived models across sessions and processing revisions.
status: Long-term recording and data standards provide components; identity uncertainty is not eliminated by assigning a stable identifier.
why: Prevents false longitudinal changes and incorrect multimodal joins.
key_works: Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`; Rübel et al. (2022), *The Neurodata Without Borders ecosystem for neurophysiological data science*, DOI: `10.7554/eLife.78362`.

title: Intervention-generalization benchmark suite
open: Build benchmarks with held-out perturbations, laboratories, animals, and behavioral conditions, requiring calibrated predictions of both neural and behavioral outcomes.
status: Neural Latents Benchmark ’21 provides standardized latent-model evaluation; extending evaluation to causal intervention generalization is a distinct target.
why: Rewards models that predict mechanisms outside their training distribution.
key_works: Pei et al. (2021), *Neural Latents Benchmark ’21: Evaluating latent variable models of neural population activity*, arXiv: `2109.04463`; Randi et al. (2023), *Neural signal propagation atlas of Caenorhabditis elegans*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06683-4`.

title: Quantifying analysis-pipeline uncertainty
open: Propagate defensible variation in preprocessing, modeling, and statistical choices into the final uncertainty of a neuroscience claim.
status: A 2020 many-team analysis of one imaging dataset demonstrated substantial analytical variability; selecting one pipeline does not remove that source of uncertainty.
why: Prevents precision estimates from ignoring researcher choices.
key_works: Botvinik-Nezer et al. (2020), *Variability in the analysis of a single neuroimaging dataset by many teams*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-020-2314-9`.

title: Usable negative-result and failed-replication datasets
open: Create standardized, searchable records of well-powered null findings, failed perturbations, and unsuccessful replications with enough metadata to distinguish informative failures from technical breakdowns.
status: Large-sample and many-analyst studies document important reliability problems; a reusable failure-data infrastructure is a further proposed target.
why: Reduces repeated dead ends and publication-driven distortions.
key_works: Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`; Botvinik-Nezer et al. (2020), *Variability in the analysis of a single neuroimaging dataset by many teams*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-020-2314-9`.

title: Sex-related mechanisms rather than average-group labels
subfield: Sex, hormonal transitions, diversity, and environment
open: Separate effects of chromosomes, hormones, development, body physiology, and social environment on a specified neural mechanism.
status: Hormone-associated structural changes demonstrate that physiological state matters; average male–female comparisons cannot independently identify the responsible causes.
why: Produces more precise biology without treating within-group variation as negligible.
key_works: Hoekzema et al. (2017), *Pregnancy leads to long-lasting changes in human brain structure*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4458`; Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`.

title: Cellular basis of pregnancy-associated brain changes
subfield: Sex, hormonal transitions, diversity, and environment
open: Determine which cellular, vascular, extracellular, and circuit changes produce pregnancy-associated imaging differences and how they relate to function.
status: Long-lasting structural changes were reported in 2017; MRI volume changes do not directly establish neuron loss, improved function, or impairment.
why: Prevents unsupported interpretations of a major human physiological transition.
key_works: Hoekzema et al. (2017), *Pregnancy leads to long-lasting changes in human brain structure*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4458`.

title: Menopause-related neural change versus chronological aging
subfield: Sex, hormonal transitions, diversity, and environment
open: Distinguish effects of ovarian hormonal transition from chronological aging, vascular change, sleep, treatment, and prior health, with longitudinal causal designs.
status: Pregnancy studies establish that endocrine transitions can accompany persistent neural changes; they do not answer the distinct menopause-specific causal problem.
why: Supports mechanism-based evaluation of symptoms and interventions.
