key_works: Hoekzema et al. (2017), *Pregnancy leads to long-lasting changes in human brain structure*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4458`; Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.

title: Gene–environment mechanisms across the life course
subfield: Sex, hormonal transitions, diversity, and environment
open: Determine how specific exposures interact with genetic and developmental state to alter neural trajectories, using exposure measurements rather than broad proxies.
status: Genetic discovery and reliable population-level brain associations have advanced separately; their mechanistic interaction remains far harder than either marginal association.
why: Connects environmental prevention to biological susceptibility.
key_works: Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`; Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`.

title: Population-inclusive neural reference models
subfield: Sex, hormonal transitions, diversity, and environment
open: Build normative models that remain calibrated across ancestry, language, disability, age, socioeconomic conditions, and acquisition sites, with explicit uncertainty for poorly represented groups.
status: Large-sample reproducibility findings establish the need for sufficient data; large sample size alone does not guarantee representative coverage or fairness.
why: Prevents reference datasets from systematically misclassifying underrepresented people.
key_works: Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`; UNESCO (2025), *Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology*.

title: Verifiable privacy for neural data
open: Design technical and governance controls that limit unauthorized inference from neural recordings, including future inferences not anticipated when data were collected.
status: UNESCO adopted its neurotechnology ethics recommendation in 2025; a normative framework does not itself provide enforceable, technically verified privacy guarantees.
why: Protects people as decoding methods and data reuse evolve.
key_works: UNESCO (2025), *Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology*; Card et al. (2024), *An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2314132`.

title: Funded lifetime obligations for neural implants
open: Establish enforceable and financed arrangements for maintenance, software support, explantation, replacement, data access, and continuity if a trial ends or a developer disappears.
status: Post-trial neural-implant obligations have been explicitly examined in neuroethics; identifying responsibilities is not the same as funding and operationalizing them.
why: Prevents participants from being left with unsupported implanted systems.
key_works: Dasgupta et al. (2024), *What Happens After a Neural Implant Study? Neuroethics Expert Workshop on Post-Trial Obligations*, DOI: `10.1007/s12152-024-09549-2`; UNESCO (2025), *Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology*.

title: Sustainable funding for shared neuroscience infrastructure
open: Create durable funding and maintenance models for standards, archives, reference datasets, and essential software, with measurable service quality and succession plans.
status: Neurodata Without Borders demonstrates the value of shared infrastructure; a functioning ecosystem does not eliminate its continuing maintenance and financing requirements.
why: Prevents foundational scientific assets from decaying between grants.
key_works: Rübel et al. (2022), *The Neurodata Without Borders ecosystem for neurophysiological data science*, DOI: `10.7554/eLife.78362`.

title: Closing neurological-care access gaps
open: Identify and finance delivery models that sustainably improve access to diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation, and essential neurological services in underserved settings.
status: The WHO intersectoral action plan supplies agreed objectives; implementation, workforce capacity, procurement, and financing remain separate, locally testable problems.
why: Converts scientific capability into actual population benefit.
key_works: World Health Organization (2022), *Intersectoral global action plan on epilepsy and other neurological disorders 2022–2031*, ISBN: `9789240076624`.

title: Adaptive consent and oversight for evolving neural capabilities
open: Develop consent and review systems that remain meaningful as neural datasets gain new uses, implants change function, and engineered neural tissues acquire more complex capabilities.
status: UNESCO’s 2025 recommendation establishes an international normative reference, while organoid integration and decoding advances change the capabilities that oversight must address.
why: Makes governance responsive to actual capability rather than fixed historical assumptions.
key_works: UNESCO (2025), *Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology*; Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`.

title: R10.01. Routing neuronal self-DNA into a memory-promoting TLR9 response
open: Identify which learning-associated DNA fragments activate neuronal TLR9, how those fragments reach the relevant intracellular compartment, and what prevents the response from becoming damaging inflammation. A solution should predict when the same DNA-sensing machinery promotes memory recruitment, has no effect, or injures the neuron.
status: A 2024 mouse study connected learning-associated DNA damage, TLR9 signaling, DNA repair, and recruitment into memory assemblies. This establishes a pathway to investigate, not a general explanation of how neurons distinguish useful self-DNA signaling from pathological innate immune activation.
why: Could separate the memory-supporting and potentially harmful consequences of neuronal DNA sensing.
key_works: Jovasevic et al. (2024), *Formation of memory assemblies through the DNA-sensing TLR9 pathway*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-024-07220-7`.

title: R10.02. Repair fidelity at repeatedly activated NPAS4–NuA4 target loci
open: Determine how the NPAS4–NuA4 complex selects damaged loci and whether repeated activity-dependent repair preserves their sequence and regulatory function over a neuron’s lifetime. Distinguish accurate repair from repair that prevents immediate death but gradually accumulates mutations or regulatory alterations.
status: The NPAS4–NuA4 connection between neuronal activity and DNA repair was established in 2023. Its protective role does not establish the cumulative fidelity of repair across repeated activation, aging, or different neuronal populations.
why: Tests whether an adaptive response to activity creates a previously hidden long-term genomic cost.
key_works: Pollina et al. (2023), *A NPAS4–NuA4 complex couples synaptic activity to DNA repair*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-05711-7`.

title: R10.03. The approximately 150-CAG transition in Huntington’s neurons
open: Determine whether the reported transition near 150 somatic HTT CAG repeats represents a causal biological threshold, a distributed set of cell-specific thresholds, or an apparent boundary influenced by sampling and selective cell loss. Predict the transition from repeat length, interruption structure, cell identity, and age.
status: A 2025 single-cell study linked extensive somatic expansion to loss of striatal projection-neuron identity, with a marked transition around 150 repeats in the sampled cells. That result should not be treated as an invariant threshold already established for every neuronal population or patient.
why: Would turn repeat measurements into mechanistically grounded estimates of proximity to neuronal failure.
key_works: Handsaker et al. (2025), *Long somatic DNA-repeat expansion drives neurodegeneration in Huntington’s disease*, PMID: `39824182`.

title: R10.04. Suppressing MSH3 without exchanging repeat expansion for other genomic damage
open: Define a tissue-specific and time-dependent intervention window in which reducing MSH3 meaningfully suppresses pathogenic repeat expansion without unacceptable accumulation of other DNA errors. Success requires measuring both repeat stabilization and broader mutation burdens over extended periods.
status: In 2025, antisense-mediated MSH3 suppression reduced somatic CAG expansion in Huntington’s disease patient-derived striatal neurons. Long-term genomic safety and the necessary degree of suppression remain separate questions from demonstrating reduced expansion in culture.
why: Establishes whether a promising repeat-expansion intervention has a usable long-term therapeutic margin.
key_works: Bunting et al. (2025), *Antisense oligonucleotide–mediated MSH3 suppression reduces somatic CAG repeat expansion in Huntington’s disease iPSC–derived striatal neurons*, DOI: `10.1126/scitranslmed.adn4600`.

title: R10.05. Selective elimination of C9orf72 cryptic translation templates
open: Quantify how much toxic dipeptide-repeat production originates from cryptically initiated intronic transcripts in each relevant human cell state, then suppress those transcripts without compromising necessary C9orf72 expression. Distinguish promoter inhibition, transcript destruction, and translation inhibition experimentally.
status: A 2025 study identified capped, intron-initiated transcripts that serve as efficient endogenous templates for repeat-associated translation. Stabilizing intron lariats through Dbr1 knockdown did not increase dipeptide-repeat production in the tested patient-derived neurons, narrowing—but not universally closing—the alternative-template question.
why: Could target the toxic expression route more selectively than indiscriminate suppression of the entire locus.
key_works: Miller et al. (2025), *Cryptic intronic transcriptional initiation generates efficient endogenous mRNA templates for C9orf72-associated RAN translation*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2507334122`.

title: R10.06. Replacing damaged neuronal nuclear pores without opening the barrier
open: Determine how aged neurons inspect, repair, and replace damaged components of exceptionally long-lived nuclear pore complexes while preserving nuclear selectivity. Establish whether defective pores can be selectively renewed without transient leakage or wholesale disruption of nuclear transport.
status: Extremely long-lived nuclear pore proteins were identified in rat brain in 2012. Component longevity does not establish that pores are immutable, nor does evidence of component exchange by itself explain safe replacement of damaged assemblies in old neurons.
why: Provides a specific intervention target for deterioration of nuclear compartmentalization.
key_works: Savas et al. (2012), *Extremely long-lived nuclear pore proteins in the rat brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1217421`.

title: R10.07. What information the axon-to-cilium serotonin synapse conveys
open: Determine whether serotonin delivered to a neuronal primary cilium carries instructions distinguishable from serotonin acting on the rest of the cell. Selectively disrupt the ciliary route while preserving nonciliary signaling, then test predicted changes in nuclear regulation and behavior.
status: An axon–cilium serotonergic synapse and a cilium-to-nucleus signaling pathway were demonstrated in 2022. The anatomical connection and chromatin effects are established findings; their behavior-specific informational role remains the narrower target.
why: Could reveal a dedicated channel through which particular inputs regulate long-term cellular programs.
key_works: Sheu et al. (2022), *A serotonergic axon-cilium synapse drives nuclear signaling to alter chromatin accessibility*, PMID: `36055200`.

title: R10.08. Reissner-fiber mechanics versus urotensin signaling in spine morphogenesis
open: Separate the contributions of Reissner-fiber tension, motion, biochemical interactions, and cerebrospinal-fluid-contacting neuronal signaling to maintenance of body-axis shape. A solution should predict which deformities follow selective mechanical disruption versus selective interruption of the downstream signaling pathway.
status: Reissner-fiber-dependent urotensin signaling was linked to prevention of spinal curvature in 2020. A September 2025 preprint reported that motile cilia rotate a tensioned, anchored fiber, adding a mechanical mechanism that must be integrated with the signaling results.
why: Connects nervous-system fluid mechanics to a concrete developmental orthopedic phenotype.
key_works: Lu et al. (2020), *Reissner fibre-induced urotensin signalling from cerebrospinal fluid-contacting neurons prevents scoliosis of vertebrate spine*, DOI: `10.1242/bio.052027`; Bearce et al. (2025), *Motile cilia spin the Reissner fiber, a tensioned and anchored extracellular thread essential for body morphogenesis*, preprint, DOI: `10.1101/2025.09.25.678623`.

title: R10.09. Recovery of ependymal ciliary coordination after local damage
open: Predict whether coordinated ciliary beating and effective ventricular flow recover after a localized patch of cilia is damaged, misoriented, or replaced. The model must distinguish cell-intrinsic polarity, neighbor interactions, and hydrodynamic coupling on the curved ventricular surface.
status: Cilia were shown to participate in organizing ependymal planar polarity in 2010. Developmental establishment of polarity is not a complete account of phase coordination, defect propagation, or repair in an already functioning ventricular surface.
why: Identifies which local defects can cause persistent disruption of cerebrospinal-fluid movement.
key_works: Mirzadeh et al. (2010), *Cilia organize ependymal planar polarity*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.3744-09.2010`.

title: R10.10. Physically consistent, independently validated chloride microdomains
open: Establish when neighboring neuronal compartments genuinely maintain different free chloride activities, rather than different sensor environments, pH, or chloride-binding conditions. Derive and test the transport, buffering, and geometrical requirements for the measured gradients to persist.
status: A 2021 study reported chloride microdomains associated with heterogeneous GABA responses. The remaining challenge is independent quantitative validation and a transport model that explains the gradients’ stability under realistic diffusion and activity.
why: Determines whether a single intracellular chloride value is an inadequate description of inhibitory signaling within one neuron.
key_works: Rahmati et al. (2021), *Unique Actions of GABA Arising from Cytoplasmic Chloride Microdomains*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.3175-20.2021`.

title: R10.11. The axonal cisternal organelle’s function, separated from the spine apparatus
open: Determine what the calcium-storing cisternal organelle contributes specifically at the axon initial segment. Selectively remove or restore it while leaving the dendritic spine apparatus intact, then measure effects on inhibition, spike initiation, and adaptation.
status: The organelle was anatomically associated with initial-segment GABAergic synapses in 1994. Synaptopodin-deficient models remove both axonal cisternal organelles and dendritic spine apparatuses; a September 2026 knockout-rat study expands experimental access but preserves this important causal-separation problem.
why: Prevents phenotypes caused by two different organelles from being attributed to either one without separation.
key_works: Benedeczky, Molnár, and Somogyi (1994), *The cisternal organelle as a Ca2+-storing compartment associated with GABAergic synapses in the axon initial segment of hippocampal pyramidal neurones*, DOI: `10.1007/BF00228742`; Kuwajima et al. (2026), *Synaptopodin KO rat for assessing the dendritic spine apparatus and axonal cisternal organelle in synaptic plasticity, development, and behavior*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pone.0355625`.

title: R10.12. Homeostatic compensation in axon-carrying-dendrite neurons
open: Explain how neurons whose axon originates from a dendrite stabilize excitability when their axon initial segment lacks the homeostatic plasticity observed in comparison neurons. Test whether compensation shifts to dendritic conductances, inhibition, synaptic scaling, or another compartment.
status: A study published online in 2024 and in a 2025 journal issue found preserved initial-segment architecture and trafficking-barrier function in cultured axon-carrying-dendrite neurons, but absent initial-segment homeostatic plasticity under the tested conditions, fewer cisternal organelles, and fewer inhibitory inputs. The barrier’s existence is therefore not the open question.
why: Tests whether a distinct neuronal geometry requires a distinct stability mechanism.
key_works: Han et al. (2025), *Unveiling the cell biology of hippocampal neurons with dendritic axon origin*, DOI: `10.1083/jcb.202403141`; Thome et al. (2014), *Axon-Carrying Dendrites Convey Privileged Synaptic Input in Hippocampal Neurons*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2014.08.013`.

title: R10.13. Dynamic regulation of the periaxonal nanocircuit
open: Measure how the nanoscale space between axon and myelin changes in geometry and ionic composition during realistic spike trains. Determine whether those changes actively regulate conduction or instead create activity-dependent failure and timing noise.
status: A 2020 study combined recordings, ultrastructure, and modeling to establish a conductive periaxonal pathway in saltatory conduction. Its existence does not settle whether nanospace width and conductivity are dynamically controlled during behavior.
why: Identifies a potential regulator of axonal timing that is distinct from changing myelin thickness or internode length.
key_works: Cohen et al. (2020), *Saltatory Conduction along Myelinated Axons Involves a Periaxonal Nanocircuit*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.11.039`.

title: R10.14. Replenishment and fate of the adult silent-filopodial synapse reserve
open: Determine whether adult filopodial silent synapses are continuously replenished, consumed by learning, recycled, or converted into long-lived spines. Quantify the reserve’s turnover and test whether its depletion limits subsequent learning.
status: In 2022, filopodia were identified as a major substrate of silent synapses in sampled adult mouse visual-cortical neurons, and their functional recruitment was demonstrated. The unresolved issue is the reserve’s long-term lifecycle, not whether adult silent synapses exist.
why: Could reveal a renewable structural resource supporting adult learning.
key_works: Vardalaki, Chung, and Harnett (2022), *Filopodia are a structural substrate for silent synapses in adult neocortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05483-6`.

title: R10.15. Regulation of opposing transmitters inside the same vesicle
open: Determine how the glutamate-to-GABA content of individual co-packaged vesicles is established and whether it changes with activity or physiological state. Predict when a release event produces net excitation, inhibition, or a timing-dependent combination at its target.
status: A 2022 study demonstrated co-packaging of glutamate and GABA in individual vesicles at a defined central synapse. Thus, co-packaging itself is not hypothetical; its stoichiometric regulation and functional flexibility are the finer-grained targets.
why: Challenges models that assign a single fixed sign to a presynaptic release event.
key_works: Kim et al. (2022), *Co-packaging of opposing neurotransmitters in individual synaptic vesicles in the central nervous system*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2022.01.007`; Kim and Sabatini (2023), *Analytical approaches to examine gamma-aminobutyric acid and glutamate vesicular co-packaging*, DOI: `10.3389/fnsyn.2022.1076616`.

title: R10.16. Arc capsid cargo selection and recipient specificity
open: Identify which endogenous RNAs are preferentially packaged into Arc particles, which cells receive them, and what transferred cargo does in those recipients. Separate intercellular transfer functions from Arc’s intracellular roles using interventions that preserve one while disrupting the other.
status: In 2018, Arc was shown to form virus-like capsids and mediate intercellular RNA transfer. These findings do not establish a complete endogenous cargo-selection code or prove which behavioral effects require transfer between cells.
why: Could identify a genetically encoded communication channel distinct from neurotransmission.
key_works: Pastuzyn et al. (2018), *The Neuronal Gene Arc Encodes a Repurposed Retrotransposon Gag Protein that Mediates Intercellular RNA Transfer*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2017.12.024`.

title: R10.17. Identities and receptors of neuronal membrane-proteasome peptides
open: Identify the physiologically released peptides produced by neuronal membrane proteasomes and establish which receptors or uptake mechanisms mediate their effects. Distinguish direct receptor binding from indirect changes in glutamate signaling or extracellular protein processing.
status: Work published in 2024 linked membrane-proteasome-derived peptides to NMDAR-dependent signaling and gene-expression changes; another study implicated membrane proteasomes in peripheral nociceptor activity. NMDAR dependence does not establish that the peptides directly bind NMDARs.
why: Could uncover a signaling system whose molecular messages remain inadequately identified.
key_works: Türker, Brennan, and Margolis (2024), *Neuronal membrane proteasome-derived peptides modulate NMDAR-dependent neuronal signaling to promote changes in gene expression*, DOI: `10.1091/mbc.E23-06-0218`; Villalón Landeros et al. (2024), *The nociceptive activity of peripheral sensory neurons is modulated by the neuronal membrane proteasome*, DOI: `10.1016/j.celrep.2024.114058`.

title: R10.18. Mitochondrial triage during transmitophagy
open: Determine how retinal ganglion-cell axons select mitochondria for transfer to optic-nerve-head astrocytes. Distinguish disposal of locally damaged mitochondria from disposal of cargo transported there, and test whether healthy organelles are ever sacrificed to relieve logistical constraints.
status: Transcellular degradation of axonal mitochondria by astrocytes was demonstrated in 2014. The discovery establishes the disposal route but not its cargo-selection rules, spatial rationale, or quality-control accuracy.
why: Explains how long axons outsource maintenance without losing essential energy-producing organelles.
key_works: Davis et al. (2014), *Transcellular degradation of axonal mitochondria*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.1404651111`.

title: R10.19. Exopher export: successful disposal or redistribution of proteotoxic risk
open: Quantify when extrusion of large neuronal cargo-containing vesicles benefits both donor and tissue, versus merely moving aggregates into recipients that cannot degrade them. Establish the corresponding balance in mammalian neural tissue rather than assuming results transfer directly from nematodes.
status: Exopher production and its association with proteostress have been studied in *C. elegans*; a 2023 study connected intermediate filaments, aggresome-like structures, and exopher extrusion. Donor-cell protection does not by itself demonstrate safe downstream disposal.
why: Determines whether promoting neuronal cargo export could protect tissue or spread a pathological burden.
key_works: Arnold et al. (2023), *Intermediate filaments associate with aggresome-like structures in proteostressed C. elegans neurons and influence large vesicle extrusions as exophers*, DOI: `10.1038/s41467-023-39700-1`.

title: R10.20. The last reversible state after SARM1 activation
open: Define the biochemical and electrophysiological boundary beyond which an axon cannot recover after SARM1 activation. Determine how that boundary changes with injury type, neuronal subtype, and duration, using restoration of conduction and synaptic output rather than survival alone.
status: A 2025 human-neuron study demonstrated reversible mitochondrial dysfunction after SARM1 activation and protection through antisense intervention. Reversibility is therefore already demonstrated in a defined setting; the open target is a predictive, transferable rescue window and proof of complete functional recovery.
why: Establishes when intervention can still rescue an existing axon rather than merely delay fragmentation.
key_works: Loreto et al. (2025), *SARM1 activation induces reversible mitochondrial dysfunction and can be prevented in human neurons by antisense oligonucleotides*, DOI: `10.1016/j.nbd.2025.106986`.

title: R10.21. Eliminating paradoxical activation by SARM1 base-exchange inhibitors
open: Determine whether SARM1 base-exchange inhibitors can be engineered to avoid activating the enzyme at partial occupancy, low exposure, or during washout. Establish whether the liability follows necessarily from particular binding mechanisms or can be removed while retaining inhibition.
status: An industrial drug-discovery program reported in May 2026 that compounds with promising inhibitory properties could activate SARM1 and accelerate neurite degeneration at subinhibitory exposure. This is a specific negative-result frontier, not evidence that every SARM1 inhibitor shares the same failure mode.
why: Prevents an intended neuroprotective treatment from becoming harmful in poorly exposed tissue or as concentrations decline.
key_works: Lundbäck et al. (2026), *The rise and fall of SARM1 base-exchange inhibitors*, DOI: `10.1038/s42004-026-02074-8`.

title: R10.22. The molecular source of horizontal-cell feedback at the cone synapse
open: Identify the transporters and local physical processes that generate horizontal-cell feedback onto cones, quantitatively separating proton/bicarbonate effects from ephaptic contributions. Resolve whether different preparations reveal different mechanisms or different operating regimes of the same mechanism.
status: Warren’s 2016 dissertation reported feedback dependence on bicarbonate-related processes and kinetics inconsistent with a purely instantaneous mechanism in the tested preparation. These results constrain candidate mechanisms but do not establish a universal, molecule-resolved account across vertebrate retinas.
why: Resolves a specific missing mechanism at the retina’s first synapse.
key_works: Warren (2016), *Mechanisms of lateral-inhibitory feedback from horizontal cells to cone photoreceptors at the first synapse of the retina*, doctoral dissertation, University of Nebraska Medical Center, thesis record `66`.

title: R10.23. The metastable visual-pigment state proposed to generate continuous dark noise
open: Identify the molecular conformation and transition kinetics of the visual-pigment state proposed to generate continuous dark noise. Predict how mutations alter this noise independently of photon sensitivity and discrete thermal activation events.
status: A 2024 study attributed an important continuous-noise component to visual pigment and proposed a metastable pigment state. The state’s detailed molecular identity remains a mechanistic target rather than a solved structural result.
why: Could explain a fundamental sensory-noise source at molecular resolution.
key_works: Chai et al. (2024), *Dark continuous noise from visual pigment as a major mechanism underlying rod–cone difference in light sensitivity*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2418031121`.

title: R10.24. Native-cone verification of the proposed pigment-noise budget
open: Test whether the proposed pigment-derived continuous noise accounts quantitatively for sensitivity and adaptation in native cones. Separate pigment noise from downstream amplification, feedback, and other spontaneous biochemical activity.
status: The 2024 work inferred approximately **2,000–6,000-fold** differences between cone and rod pigments under matched-expression comparisons using engineered experimental systems. That is not a direct measurement of an equivalent noise ratio in native human cones.
why: Tests whether a striking molecular explanation survives transfer to the intact sensory cell.
key_works: Chai et al. (2024), the visual-pigment continuous-noise study identified in R10.23, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2418031121`.

title: R10.25. The downstream use of suppressed-by-contrast retinal ganglion cells
open: Determine whether suppressed-by-contrast ganglion cells causally help distinguish self-generated visual changes from external events. Identify their downstream readers and predict behavioral consequences of selectively altering their suppression signals.
status: In 2015, a genetically identified population reliably signaled stimuli resembling saccades and blinks, with specific excitatory and inhibitory mechanisms characterized. Reliable signaling of those stimuli is established; necessity for perceptual stabilization is the remaining target.
why: Links an unusual retinal response class to a concrete computation rather than leaving it as a physiological curiosity.
key_works: Tien et al. (2015), *Genetically Identified Suppressed-by-Contrast Retinal Ganglion Cells Reliably Signal Self-Generated Visual Stimuli*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1521-15.2015`.

title: R10.26. Allocation between parallel cone visual cycles in human daylight
open: Quantify the contributions of Müller-cell and retinal-pigment-epithelium pathways to cone pigment regeneration during realistic spectral and intensity changes. Predict when one route compensates for another and when the combined system becomes rate-limiting.
status: A 2019 study established a light-driven regeneration mechanism involving RGR opsin in Müller glia. Its existence is not open; the unresolved target is quantitative pathway allocation, particularly in human daylight conditions and across species with different retinal organization.
why: Identifies which regeneration bottlenecks actually limit sustained cone vision.
key_works: Morshedian et al. (2019), *Light-Driven Regeneration of Cone Visual Pigments through a Mechanism Involving RGR Opsin in Müller Glial Cells*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2019.04.004`.

title: R10.27. Can artificial cone-subpopulation signals create an additional learned chromatic dimension?
open: Determine whether independently addressing subsets within a cone class can support a learned perceptual distinction that cannot be reduced to ordinary color coordinates or spatial texture. Success requires generalization across new spatial arrangements and controls that exclude brightness and pattern cues.
status: The 2025 Oz study demonstrated colors outside the ordinary natural gamut through selective cone stimulation. An expanded gamut, including the reported “olo” percept, is not by itself evidence of an additional independent dimension of color vision.
why: Tests whether adult visual processing can acquire a new sensory coordinate rather than merely experience unusually strong activation of existing coordinates.
key_works: Fong et al. (2025), *Novel color via stimulation of individual photoreceptors at population scale*, DOI: `10.1126/sciadv.adu1052`.

title: R10.28. Tenfold scaling of individually addressed, spectrally typed cones
open: Scale controlled stimulation from roughly **10³ to 10⁴ individually typed cones**, while holding cross-activation, retinal exposure, tracking failures, and perceptual reproducibility to predefined acceptance limits. This is a proposed engineering target, not a published performance claim.
status: The 2025 Oz prototype operated at approximately the thousand-cone scale and demonstrated image and video stimuli. Scaling spatial coverage without losing cone-level targeting is a different problem from demonstrating the initial percept.
why: Would make richer tests of neural adaptation to artificial sensory channels possible.
key_works: Fong et al. (2025), the Oz study identified in R10.27, DOI: `10.1126/sciadv.adu1052`.

title: R10.29. Resolving what L1CAM isolation actually captures in human biofluids
open: Establish when L1CAM-based isolation yields neuron-derived extracellular vesicles rather than soluble protein, non-neuronal material, or mixed contaminants. Resolve discrepancies using matched samples, orthogonal isolation methods, single-vesicle colocalization, and independently validated cellular-origin markers.
status: A 2021 study argued against L1CAM as a neuronal-vesicle isolation marker; a 2024 single-vesicle study supported its use; a 2025 study again found that most L1CAM was not vesicle-associated in the examined systems. The disagreement must be reconciled at the assay level rather than settled by citing only one side.
why: Determines whether an important class of purported brain-derived liquid biopsies measures what it claims.
key_works: Norman et al. (2021), *L1CAM is not associated with extracellular vesicles in human cerebrospinal fluid or plasma*, DOI: `10.1038/s41592-021-01174-8`; Nogueras-Ortiz et al. (2024), *Single-extracellular vesicle (EV) analyses validate the use of L1 Cell Adhesion Molecule (L1CAM) as a reliable biomarker of neuron-derived EVs*, PMID: `38868956`; Kadam et al. (2025), *Most L1CAM Is not Associated with Extracellular Vesicles in Human Biofluids and iPSC-Derived Neurons*, DOI: `10.1007/s12035-025-04909-2`.

title: R10.30. The competence boundary for PTBP1-based astrocyte reprogramming
open: Determine whether any reproducibly defined mature-astrocyte state undergoes genuine neuronal conversion after PTBP1 loss, or establish a bounded negative result across those states. Positive claims must demonstrate irreversible lineage, durable neuronal physiology, and exclusion of pre-existing neurons or labeling artifacts.
status: A 2025 study found that PTBP1 depletion in lineage-traced mature astrocytes altered splicing without broadly producing neuronal features. The next problem is not to repeat an unqualified conversion claim, but to identify the actual competence boundary—or explain why PTBP1 removal is insufficient.
why: Prevents a potentially misleading regeneration strategy from advancing on ambiguous cell-labeling evidence.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2025), *PTBP1 depletion in mature astrocytes reveals distinct splicing alterations without neuronal features*, eLife research report `107683`; preprint DOI: `10.1101/2025.05.30.657115`.

title: R10.31. In-situ attribution of dopamine and norepinephrine sensor signals
open: Recover the contributions of dopamine and norepinephrine to a fluorescent sensor signal in each tissue context. Establish when calibration and complementary measurements make the decomposition identifiable, and when the correct output is an explicit statement of ambiguity.
status: An August 2026 study showed that cross-reactivity of dopamine and norepinephrine sensors depends on local innervation density. Selectivity measured in a simplified expression system is therefore insufficient to assign transmitter identity in every brain region.
why: Prevents a transmitter-specific causal story from being built on a mixed chemical signal.
key_works: López et al. (2026), *Norepinephrine and dopamine sensor crosstalk depends on local innervation density*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-026-02379-w`.

title: R10.32. Separating direct ultrasound neuromodulation from cochlear recruitment
open: Define conditions under which a measured neural or behavioral effect is attributable to direct target modulation rather than activation through the auditory system. Require simultaneous target-engagement measurements and controls capable of detecting residual cochlear contributions.
status: A 2018 study demonstrated extensive ultrasound-induced activation through a cochlear pathway. A 2025 awake-brain study measured rapid membrane-potential effects, strengthening evidence for direct modulation under specific conditions. Neither result establishes one explanation for all ultrasound protocols.
why: Establishes whether an apparent deep-brain intervention actually acts through its intended route.
key_works: Guo et al. (2018), *Ultrasound Produces Extensive Brain Activation via a Cochlear Pathway*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2018.04.036`; Bortz et al. (2025), *Transcranial ultrasound stimulation modulates neuronal membrane potentials across broad timescales in the awake mammalian brain*, DOI: `10.1016/j.brs.2025.09.004`.

title: R10.33. Quantitative partition of central and peripheral tACS effects
open: Estimate what fraction of a transcranial alternating-current stimulation effect arises from direct brain fields versus stimulation of peripheral nerves. Predict that partition across anatomies and tasks instead of assuming that either mechanism always dominates.
status: In 2019, one study demonstrated that motor-system effects could arise through peripheral nerves, while another demonstrated entrainment of primate single-neuron activity. The useful unresolved question is context-dependent causal contribution, not a binary claim that direct or indirect effects never occur.
why: Makes stimulation results interpretable and improves targeting.
key_works: Asamoah, Khatoun, and McLaughlin (2019), *tACS motor system effects can be caused by transcutaneous stimulation of peripheral nerves*, PMID: `30655523`; Krause et al. (2019), *Transcranial alternating current stimulation entrains single-neuron activity in the primate brain*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.1815958116`.

title: R10.34. Edge-specific detection probabilities in rabies connectivity tracing
open: Estimate the probability that an existing synaptic connection is labeled as a function of cell type, synapse properties, starter-cell state, and experimental conditions. Validate those probabilities against independently measured connectivity rather than treating labeled-cell counts as direct connection strengths.
status: A 2023 quantitative analysis examined important limitations of rabies-based connectivity tracing. The remaining target is a transferable calibration of missing and preferentially detected edges, not merely a larger traced network.
why: Converts a powerful anatomical technique into a better-calibrated quantitative measurement.
key_works: Tran-Van-Minh, Ye, and Rancz (2023), *Quantitative analysis of rabies virus-based synaptic connectivity tracing*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pone.0278053`.

title: R10.35. Density-invariant population statistics from ultra-high-density probes
open: Recover neuronal counts, cell-class proportions, correlations, and synchrony after correcting for probe-density-dependent detection and axon-versus-soma sampling. Establish when two detected units correspond to independent neurons versus different observable parts of a single cell.
status: Neuropixels Ultra increased recording yield by more than twofold in the reported mouse visual-cortex comparison and improved identification from spatial electrical footprints. These gains do not automatically make the detected population an unbiased sample of local neurons.
why: Prevents better instruments from changing apparent biological conclusions through altered sampling alone.
key_works: Ye et al. (2025), *Ultra-high-density Neuropixels probes improve detection and identification in neuronal recordings*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2025.08.030`.

title: R10.36. Causal leaders and replacement rules in the GnRH pulse generator
open: Determine whether early-recruited kisspeptin neurons causally initiate a hormone pulse or merely report a distributed transition. Predict whether removing an apparent leader suppresses pulses, changes their timing, or causes another cell to assume its role.
status: In-vivo imaging in 2022 revealed temporal recruitment order within the pulse generator, and subsequent work examined synchronization mechanisms. Observed ordering does not by itself establish a fixed pacemaker hierarchy or its resilience to cell loss.
why: Distinguishes a replaceable distributed oscillator from a small set of indispensable initiators.
key_works: Moore et al. (2022), *In vivo imaging of the GnRH pulse generator reveals a temporal order of neuronal activation and synchronization during each pulse*, PMID: `35110409`; Han et al. (2023), *Mechanism of kisspeptin neuron synchronization for pulsatile hormone secretion in male mice*, Cell Reports 42, article `111914`.

title: R10.37. Steroid-dependent integration of opposing monoaminergic inputs to reproductive pulses
open: Predict how norepinephrine and serotonin jointly alter kisspeptin-network pulse timing across gonadal-steroid states. Distinguish direct integration within the pulse generator from changes mediated through other physiological systems.
status: A 2025 study found strong, state-dependent noradrenergic suppression of the mouse kisspeptin pulse generator. A 2026 study reported robust serotonergic activation. The combined transfer function under physiological coactivation is not established by studying each input separately.
why: Could explain why similar stress or pharmacological inputs have different reproductive effects in different endocrine states.
key_works: Vas et al. (2025), *Brainstem noradrenergic modulation of the kisspeptin neuron GnRH pulse generator in mice*, DOI: `10.1038/s41467-025-60837-8`; Morris et al. (2026), *Robust serotonin activation of the kisspeptin GnRH pulse generator in male and female mice*, DOI: `10.1093/endo/bqag034`.

title: R10.38. The molecular message from cerebrospinal fluid to skull marrow
open: Identify which cerebrospinal-fluid molecules instruct particular skull-marrow progenitors and immune-cell populations after a defined neural injury. Determine whether the resulting response preserves spatial information about the injury or is simply a generalized inflammatory signal.
status: Direct cerebrospinal-fluid access to skull bone-marrow niches through dural channels, together with injury-associated marrow responses, was demonstrated in 2022. The route exists; the unresolved target is the specific message, recipient program, and distinction from circulating signals.
why: Could make local neuroimmune recruitment selectively controllable without suppressing systemic immunity.
key_works: Mazzitelli et al. (2022), *Cerebrospinal fluid regulates skull bone marrow niches via direct access through dural channels*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-022-01029-1`.

title: R10.39. Biological learning versus decoder adaptation in cultured-neuron computing
open: Determine how much task improvement comes from changes inside living neural tissue rather than adaptation of an electronic decoder, fixed reservoir dynamics, or changes in stimulation statistics. Require fixed-readout and matched-control conditions, plus selective disruption of the proposed biological plasticity mechanism.
status: DishBrain in 2022 and Brainoware in 2023 reported task-relevant behavior or computation using living neural preparations. These demonstrations motivate—but do not replace—a causal accounting of which component learned and what was retained. Claims about “sentience” are not required to formulate or solve this technical problem.
why: Establishes whether living tissue provides adaptive computation beyond what a fixed nonlinear substrate and trained readout would deliver.
key_works: Kagan et al. (2022), *In vitro neurons learn and exhibit sentience when embodied in a simulated game-world*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2022.09.001`; Cai et al. (2023), *Brain organoid reservoir computing for artificial intelligence*, DOI: `10.1038/s41928-023-01069-w`.

title: R10.40. End-to-end efficiency advantage for living neural computing
open: Demonstrate a **proposed tenfold improvement** in energy or total operating cost per successfully completed task against a specified electronic baseline, including incubation, fluid handling, amplifiers, stimulation, training, failed cultures, and replacement. Match task accuracy, throughput, and availability rather than comparing isolated neuronal energy consumption.
status: Brainoware demonstrated organoid-based reservoir computation in 2023. That is not an end-to-end demonstration of a tenfold efficiency advantage after all supporting equipment and biological maintenance are included.
why: Determines whether biological computing has a practical advantage rather than an attractive comparison at only one system boundary.
key_works: Cai et al. (2023), *Brain organoid reservoir computing for artificial intelligence*, DOI: `10.1038/s41928-023-01069-w`.

title: R10.41. Counterfactual multimodal tests for brain-encoding models
open: Build a benchmark in which visual scenes, dialogue, subtitles, and soundtracks are systematically recombined so that ordinarily correlated cues disagree. Require models to predict neural responses to these conflicts without refitting, separating genuine cross-modal computation from exploitation of natural-movie correlations.
status: Algonauts 2025 supplied a substantial naturalistic multimodal brain-prediction challenge. Its existence and results do not establish performance on controlled modality conflicts, causal cue substitutions, or other counterfactual stimulus combinations.
why: Exposes models that predict ordinary movies well while attributing a brain response to the wrong input modality.
key_works: Gifford et al. (2025), *The Algonauts Project 2025 Challenge: How the Human Brain Makes Sense of Multimodal Movies*, arXiv: `2501.00504`; Algonauts Project, official 2025 challenge rules, results, and CCN workshop materials.
prize: **Related completed competition, not an active bounty for this proposed extension:** Algonauts 2025 advertised cash prizes of **€7,500, €5,000, and €3,000** for its top three teams. Its submission period closed in July 2025.
